3.1 For $p\notin Z$, choose a basis neighborhood $B\ni p$ with $e(B)<\varepsilon$. Its actual energies are below $\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large indices. Choose a smaller disk or physical-boundary half-disk about $p$ whose closure lies in $B$. Step 1.1 bounds the gradients uniformly on a neighborhood of $p$. Finite subcovers give uniform local $C^1$ bounds on every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$. Compactness of $X$ and these derivative bounds give a further subsequence converging locally uniformly to a continuous $u_\infty$. To make the selection precise under Countable Choice, fix finite $2^{-k}$ nets of $X$ for all positive integers $k$, using Countable Choice once for this family, and a countable dense set of source points outside $Z$. At each such point use the fixed nets to extract a convergent subsequence by retaining the first net ball containing infinitely many remaining values, with radii tending to zero, and then least indices; diagonalize over the source points. One may instead use successive finite intersections of the previously retained value sets, so the centers need not form nested balls: their radii tending to zero makes the retained values Cauchy. Local equicontinuity and completeness of compact $X$ extend the dense-point limits uniquely and give uniform convergence on compact subsets, by finite source nets. Thus no arbitrary family of pointwise choices or dependent-choice axiom is needed. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct]

4.1 Higher bounds can now be obtained in genuine target charts. At an interior source point choose a target chart about its limiting image and make one constant linear coordinate change taking the limiting complex structure at that point to $i$. Local uniform convergence, uniform first-derivative bounds, and convergence of $J_n$ show that on a sufficiently small source disk all large-index images lie in one relatively compact coordinate set and the transformed coefficient differs from $i$ by at most $1/2$. At a boundary point first take an adapted target chart in which $L_j$ is real and the fixed boundary structure is $i$ along it. Here is its construction: in arbitrary target coordinates write $x\mapsto\ell(x)$ for a local parametrization of $L_j$ and set $$F(x,y)=\ell(x)+\sum_{a=1}^m y_aJ_{b,j}(\ell(x))\partial_{x_a}\ell(x).$$ Its derivative at $y=0$ maps the real and imaginary coordinate vectors to a tangent basis and its $J_{b,j}$ image. Total reality makes it invertible; [F3] gives a smooth local inverse. Consequently $F^{-1}$ sends $L_j$ to the real plane and intertwines $J_{b,j}$ with $i$ along it. At the upper strip edge use the reflected structure from step 1.1. Uniform convergence then gives the same coefficient smallness and bounded image in a fixed chart on a small half-disk. All transformed coefficient derivatives are uniformly bounded on these patches, and the coordinate first derivatives of the maps are bounded by step 3.1. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Apply [F2] on every patch of step 4.1. It gives uniform bounds for every derivative on smaller patches. Choose a countable such patch cover, possible by second countability of the strip and Countable Choice for witnessing patches. Extract one subsequence on which coordinate derivatives of every order converge locally uniformly on all these patches: use a countable dense set in each patch, bounded finite-dimensional derivative values, the deterministic bounded-sequence extraction of step 2.1, and diagonalize over patches and multi-indices. Uniform bounds of the next derivative give equicontinuity of the derivatives under consideration, so dense-point convergence is locally uniform. Integrating derivatives along coordinate segments shows that the limiting derivative functions are the derivatives of the already determined continuous limit. The limits agree on chart overlaps because their underlying maps converge to the same $u_\infty$ and the smooth coordinate change obeys the chain rule. This proves all the stated local $C^\infty$ convergence, including the half-disk boundary derivatives. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Pass to the limit in the equation using the $C^1$ convergence of the maps and local $C^\infty$ convergence of the coefficients. Closedness of the compact submanifolds $L_j$ preserves the boundary condition. On every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$, convergence of first derivatives gives convergence of the energy densities and hence an energy integral at most $E_0$. Exhaust the punctured strip by an increasing sequence of compact subsets; monotone convergence gives total limit energy at most $E_0$. None of these arguments controls what happens at the omitted finite set or at either strip end, so precisely the stated compactness conclusion follows. [step 2.1, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Use a compact target $(X,g)$, fixed compact totally real boundary submanifolds, and smooth strip equations $J_n$ with uniform bounds of every order, fixed boundary complex structures, and local $C^\infty$ convergence to $J_\infty$. Let smooth solutions $u_n$ have energies at most $E_0$. Suppose $p_n\to p$ in the strip, including its boundary, and $|du_n(p_n)|_g\to\infty$.

After taking a subsequence, translations and positive conformal dilations about points tending to $p$ give a nonconstant smooth map $v$ on either $\mathbb C$ or the closed upper half-plane, satisfying the autonomous equation $v_s+J_\infty(p,v)v_t=0$, with energy at most $E_0$. In the half-plane case its real-axis boundary lies in the boundary submanifold at $p$. Its derivative has norm one at some finite point, and its derivative norm is at most two everywhere. There is a constant $\hbar>0$ depending only on the uniform geometric data, independent of the sequence, such that $E(v)\ge\hbar$.

At the upper strip edge an orientation-preserving half-plane coordinate is used. No extension of $v$ over infinity, sphere or disk compactification, energy identity, or bubble-tree statement is asserted.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** Countable Choice, the compact geometric data and families, bounded-energy solutions, and derivative concentration in the statement.

[F1] The local interior and boundary small-energy gradient estimates are [[lem-interior-energy-regularity-for-smooth-almost-complex-strips]] and [[lem-boundary-energy-regularity-for-totally-real-strips]], with uniform comparison to the fixed metric $g$.

[F2] Uniform coordinate $C^1$ bounds give all local derivative bounds by [[lem-local-sobolev-bootstrap-for-almost-complex-strips]]. The explicit target-chart construction and countable dense-point and derivative diagonal extractions are proved in [[lem-smooth-strip-compactness-away-from-energy-concentration]].

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 Choose a flat source coordinate about $p$, centered there, with domain a disk or an upper half-disk. At the lower strip edge use the usual coordinate; at the upper edge use $z\mapsto i-z$, so both coordinates are orientation preserving and preserve the form of the equation. Write $f_n=|du_n|_g$ in this coordinate and $M_n=f_n(p_n)\to\infty$. After a tail, choose radii $$r_n=\sqrt{|p_n-p|+M_n^{-1}}$$ smaller than a fixed coordinate radius. Then $r_n\to0$, $|p_n-p|/r_n\to0$, and $r_nM_n\to\infty$. On the compact disk or half-disk of radius $r_n$ maximize $(r_n-|z|)f_n(z)$, and let $q_n$ be a maximum point. Put $\lambda_n=f_n(q_n)$ and $\delta_n=(r_n-|q_n|)/2$. The maximum is at least $(r_n-|p_n|)M_n$, so $\lambda_n\delta_n\to\infty$, and in particular $\lambda_n\to\infty$. On $B_{\delta_n}(q_n)$ intersected with the physical source half-plane, maximality gives $f_n\le2\lambda_n$. All selected points tend to $p$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $p$ is interior, rescale by $z\mapsto q_n+z/\lambda_n$. The domains contain disks about zero of radii $\lambda_n\delta_n\to\infty$; the rescaled derivatives are at most two there and have norm one at zero. If $p$ is a boundary point, write $h_n=\lambda_n\operatorname{Im}q_n\ge0$. Pass either to $h_n\to\infty$ or to a bounded sequence converging to $h\ge0$. In the first case use the same center rescaling; its boundary recedes to height $-h_n$, so the limit domain is the plane. In the second case rescale about the boundary foot $\operatorname{Re}q_n$, obtaining upper half-plane domains on which the derivative bound holds on expanding disks centered at $ih_n$. Every fixed compact upper-half-plane set eventually lies in these disks, and the derivative norm is one at $ih_n$. The boundary values remain on the original fixed submanifold. In all cases the rescaled almost complex structures converge locally smoothly to $J_*(x)=J_\infty(p,x)$: each positive source derivative gains a factor $\lambda_n^{-1}$ and the unscaled source points tend to $p$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 These rescaled maps have a subsequence converging smoothly on compact subsets of their limiting plane or half-plane. Here the details of [F2] apply without removing points: the global derivative bound two already gives local equicontinuity everywhere. Compact target finite nets and a countable dense subset of the limiting domain give a locally uniform subsequence. In a small disk about each limiting source point choose the fixed target coordinates of [F2], normalizing $J_*$ to $i$ at the center; at boundary points use its explicit totally real chart. Locally uniform convergence and smooth coefficient convergence then give the coefficient bound $\|J-i\|\le1/2$ and uniform coordinate $C^1$ bounds on a smaller fixed patch. The bootstrap in [F2] gives bounds of every order there. Its countable derivative diagonal construction yields local $C^\infty$ convergence on an exhaustion of the entire limiting domain, including boundary derivatives. Thus no concentration point remains in this selected scale. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Let $v$ be the limit. The equation and boundary condition pass to the limit. Its derivative norm is one at zero in the plane-center case, and at $ih$ in the bounded-height case: convergence is $C^1$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of those moving points. Its derivative norm is at most two by the same convergence, so it is nonconstant. A translation and dilation of a two-dimensional source preserves Dirichlet energy, since the squared derivative scaling cancels the area scaling. Therefore every compact-region energy of the rescaled maps is at most $E_0$, and passage to the smooth limit followed by exhaustion gives $E(v)\le E_0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Finally choose fixed constants $r_*>0$, $\varepsilon_*>0$, and $C_*>0$ giving the interior center and boundary half-radius supremum estimates of [F1] in the metric $g$, uniformly for every possible autonomous limit $J_*$. This is possible from the uniform coefficient bounds and the two fixed boundary structures; decrease $r_*$ below $1/4$ if necessary. If a derivative-norm-one point of $v$ in the plane, or in the half-plane at height at least $r_*/4$, is considered, apply the interior estimate on a radius-$r_*/8$ disk about it. If its half-plane height is below $r_*/4$, apply the boundary supremum estimate on the radius-$r_*$ half-disk centered at its boundary foot. If total energy is at least $\varepsilon_*$ there is already a positive lower bound. Otherwise the relevant small-energy estimate gives $$1\le\frac{64C_*}{r_*^2}E(v).$$ Consequently $$\hbar=\min\{\varepsilon_*,r_*^2/(64C_*)\}>0$$ is a uniform lower bound for the energy of this nonconstant bubble. This proves exactly the asserted plane or half-plane result, without filling its point at infinity. [F1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and $2<p<\infty$. There are constants $\eta_{m,p}>0$ and $C_{m,p}<\infty$ with the following property. Let $w\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C^m)$ have compact support, let $A$ be a bounded measurable real linear endomorphism-valued coefficient with $\|A\|_\infty\le\eta_{m,p}$, and let $f\in L^2\cap L^p$. If
$$D_0w:=w_s+iw_t=Aw_t+f$$
weakly, then $w\in W^{1,p}$ and $\|\nabla w\|_p\le C_{m,p}\|f\|_p$.

The same assertion holds on the upper half-plane if $w$ has compact support in its closure and is continuous there with real boundary values. The coefficient need not be differentiable. In particular, localizing a continuous $W^{1,2}$ map satisfying this equation on a disk or real-boundary half-disk gives local $W^{1,p}$ regularity whenever its localized forcing belongs to $L^2\cap L^p$.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** Countable Choice and the exponent, dimension, coefficient, weak solution, support, and forcing in the statement.

[F1] Smooth homogeneous degree-zero symbols on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ with bounded derivatives on its unit circle define bounded $L^p$ multipliers for $1<p<\infty$ by [[thm-mihlin-fourier-multiplier-theorem]], which assumes only Countable Choice and retains the ordinary $L^2$ Fourier-multiplier action.

[F2] Smooth compactly supported functions are dense in $W^{k,q}(\mathbb R^2)$ for finite $q$, under Countable Choice, by [[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]]. Its cutoff and mollification construction can approximate an $L^2\cap L^p$ function in both norms simultaneously.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 With Fourier convention $\widehat{\partial_jw}=2\pi i\xi_j\widehat w$, set $$r_s(\xi)=\frac{i\xi_s}{i\xi_s-\xi_t},\qquad r_t(\xi)=\frac{i\xi_t}{i\xi_s-\xi_t}\quad(\xi\ne0).$$ Both symbols are smooth and homogeneous of degree zero, and their first two derivatives are bounded on the unit circle because the denominator there has modulus one. Homogeneity gives the required Mihlin estimates. Let $R_s,R_t$ be their componentwise multiplier operators. By [F1] their $L^p$ norms on the finite-dimensional vector-valued space are bounded by a finite constant $K=K_{m,p}\ge1$, while their $L^2$ norms are at most one since $|r_s|,|r_t|\le1$. For smooth compactly supported $w$, Fourier differentiation gives $w_j=R_jD_0w$. Approximation in $W^{1,2}$ by [F2] proves the same identities for the given weak $w$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose $\eta_{m,p}=1/(2K)$. The equation and step 1.1 give $$w_t=R_tAw_t+R_tf$$ as an $L^2$ identity. The real linear operator $R_tA$ has norm at most $1/2$ on both $L^2$ and $L^p$. Therefore the geometric series $$\sum_{k\ge0}(R_tA)^kR_tf$$ converges in each of those spaces. Its partial sums belong to their intersection and have identical distributional meanings: the $L^2$ and $L^p$ multipliers agree on that intersection, because common smooth approximations from [F2] converge in both norms and the multiplier is bounded in each. The two limits thus represent the same distribution. Uniqueness of the $L^2$ solution to $(I-R_tA)v=R_tf$ identifies that limit with the already existing derivative $w_t$. Consequently $\|w_t\|_p\le2K\|f\|_p$. The equation then gives $w_s=(A-i)w_t+f\in L^p$ with a uniform bound, proving $\|\nabla w\|_p\le C_{m,p}\|f\|_p$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The function itself lies in $L^p$. Take a square $[-R,R]^2$ containing its support. The distributional identity $\partial_sw=w_s\in L^p$, together with Fubini, gives the one-dimensional primitive formula on almost every horizontal line: subtract $\int_{-R-1}^s w_s(r,t)dr$ from $w(s,t)$; its distributional $s$ derivative is zero, so it is a constant. A distribution with derivative zero is constant because it annihilates every integral-zero compact test, each of which is a derivative of a compactly supported test. The vanishing of $w$ before its support makes that constant zero. Thus Holder on each finite horizontal interval gives $\|w\|_p\le(2R+2)\|w_s\|_p$. In particular $w\in W^{1,p}$. This argument requires no general ACL or Morrey theorem. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 In the half-plane case let $C$ denote componentwise complex conjugation and extend $w$ by $\widehat w(s,-t)=Cw(s,t)$ for $t>0$. This is a compactly supported $W^{1,2}$ map on the plane. To verify the boundary claim directly, apply the primitive argument of step 3.1 on almost every vertical line; the continuous boundary values agree with the resulting finite-endpoint primitive limits. Since these values are real, the reflected values match, and integrating by parts on the two sides leaves no line atom. Define $\widehat A(s,-t)=-CA(s,t)C$ and $\widehat f(s,-t)=Cf(s,t)$, preserving their original values for $t>0$. Then $D_0\widehat w=\widehat A\widehat w_t+\widehat f$ weakly, since below the line $D_0\widehat w=C(D_0w)$ and $\widehat w_t=-Cw_t$; continuity again removes any distributional boundary term. The coefficient norm is unchanged. Apply the plane result and restrict back. Both the reflected forcing norm and derivative norm gain the same factor $2^{1/p}$, so the derivative estimate has the same constants. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 For a local equation multiply the solution by a real smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in a smaller disk or half-disk and extend it by zero. The product obeys $$D_0(\chi w)=A\partial_t(\chi w)+\chi f+(\chi_s+i\chi_t-A\chi_t)w.$$ The cutoff preserves real boundary values, and its forcing has the claimed integrability whenever the displayed localized terms do. The plane or half-plane result proves the local assertion on the region where $\chi=1$. This completes the weak regularity statement, without assuming differentiability of $A$ or regularity of the weak solution beyond the stated hypotheses. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $p>2$, $\alpha=1-2/p$, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space. Every $f\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^2;V)$ has a unique continuous representative, and
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le C_{p,V}|x-y|^\alpha\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}.$$
The same holds on the closed upper half-plane, with its gradient norm and a possibly larger constant. On a disk $B_{2r}$, or upper half-disk $B_{2r}^+$ including its straight boundary, a $W^{1,p}$ map has a continuous representative on the smaller closed disk or half-disk and satisfies
$$\|f\|_{L^\infty(B_r^{(+)})}+r^\alpha[f]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_r^{(+)}})}\le C_{p,V}\bigl(r^{-2/p}\|f\|_{L^p(B_{2r}^{(+)})}+r^{1-2/p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(B_{2r}^{(+)})}\bigr).$$
The same local conclusion applied to the weak first derivatives implies that a $W^{2,p}$ map has a $C^{1,\alpha}$ representative locally, including the straight boundary.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** Countable Choice, $p>2$, the finite-dimensional target, and the domains in the statement.

[F1] Under Countable Choice, compactly supported smooth functions are dense in $W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^2)$ by [[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]]. Approximation is componentwise in $V$.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 First take smooth $f$ and distinct points $x,y$ in the plane, and write $d=|x-y|$ and $G=B_{2d}(x)$. For either $a=x$ or $a=y$, the disk $G$ is star shaped about $a$ and is contained in $B_{4d}(a)$. In polar coordinates about $a$, its radial extent is some $R(\theta)\le4d$. The fundamental theorem of calculus along each segment gives $$\begin{aligned}|f(a)-f_G|&\le\frac1{|G|}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{R(\theta)}\rho\int_0^\rho|\nabla f(a+t e_\theta)|\,dt\,d\rho\,d\theta\\&\le\frac{(4d)^2}{2|G|}\int_G\frac{|\nabla f(z)|}{|z-a|}\,dz\le\frac2\pi\int_G\frac{|\nabla f(z)|}{|z-a|}\,dz,\end{aligned}$$ where $f_G$ denotes its average. If $p'=p/(p-1)<2$, Holder and polar integration give $$\left(\int_{B_{4d}(a)}|z-a|^{-p'}dz\right)^{1/p'}=\left(\frac{2\pi(4d)^{2-p'}}{2-p'}\right)^{1/p'}=C_p d^\alpha.$$ Adding the bounds for $a=x,y$ proves the global seminorm estimate for smooth $f$. The identical polar argument with $G=B_1(a)$ gives $|f(a)|\le\pi^{-1/p}\|f\|_{L^p(B_1(a))}+C_p\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(B_1(a))}$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Approximate a given plane $W^{1,p}$ map by smooth compactly supported $f_n$ using [F1]. The last estimate in step 1.1 applied to $f_n-f_k$ bounds its supremum on the entire plane by $C_p\|f_n-f_k\|_{W^{1,p}}$. Thus the sequence converges uniformly to a continuous map $F$. Its $L^p$ limit is $f$, so $F=f$ almost everywhere. Passing to the limit in the two-point estimate proves the claimed seminorm bound. Two continuous representatives equal almost everywhere are equal everywhere, since any point of inequality has a neighborhood of positive measure. No pointwise representative choice at uncountably many points has been made. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For the upper half-plane extend $f$ evenly: $Ef(s,-t)=f(s,t)$. This extension belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^2)$, with derivative formulas $(Ef)_s=E(f_s)$ and $(Ef)_t(s,-t)=-f_t(s,t)$, and its function and gradient norms are multiplied by $2^{1/p}$. Here is a weak justification which does not assume a trace theorem. On almost every vertical line, Fubini applied to the distributional normal derivative shows that $f(s,t)$ is represented on finite intervals by a primitive of $f_t(s,t)$ plus a constant: after subtracting that primitive, its distributional derivative vanishes, and every integral-zero test is the derivative of a compactly supported test. Since $f_t$ is integrable to $t=0$ on almost every bounded vertical interval, this primitive has a finite endpoint limit. On a bounded tangential interval the endpoint values are integrable: the primitive formula bounds their absolute values by $\int_0^1(|f|+|f_t|)dt$ after reducing to a unit-height rectangle. Its even extension matches that endpoint and the two integrations by parts have cancelling boundary terms. This proves the normal derivative formula. For the tangential formula, pair tests on the two half-planes and use the original weak tangential derivative; cut the paired test off for $t<\varepsilon$. No derivative of this cutoff occurs in the tangential integration, so convergence in $L^p$ gives the formula as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The plane result restricted to the closed half-plane now supplies the representative and estimate. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Rescale the local disk or half-disk to radius two. Choose a fixed smooth real cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on the radius-one closed disk and supported in the radius-two disk. Multiplication by $\chi$ and extension by zero gives a plane $W^{1,p}$ map in the disk case, or a half-plane $W^{1,p}$ map in the half-disk case. This follows directly from the weak product rule, because the cutoff vanishes in a neighborhood of the circular edge; at the physical straight edge no zero extension is used. Its norm is at most $C(\|f\|_p+\|\nabla f\|_p)$ on the original radius-two domain. Steps 1.1 through 3.1 give the unit-scale supremum and seminorm bound. Scaling back uses $\|f(r\cdot)\|_p=r^{-2/p}\|f\|_p$ and $\|\nabla(f(r\cdot))\|_p=r^{1-2/p}\|\nabla f\|_p$, proving precisely the displayed local estimate. Representatives on overlapping smaller domains agree by their almost-everywhere equality and continuity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Finally let $f\in W^{2,p}$ locally. Apply the local result to $f$ and each weak first derivative to obtain continuous representatives $F,G_s,G_t$ with the asserted Holder bounds on smaller domains. The distributional equalities $\partial_jF=G_j$ imply classical differentiability in the interior: convolution on an interior disk gives smooth functions whose values and first derivatives converge locally uniformly to $F,G_j$, and the fundamental theorem along segments passes to their limits. In a half-disk the resulting first derivatives extend continuously to the straight boundary; the fundamental theorem on interior segments passes to boundary segments by translation into the half-plane and continuity. Thus the representative is $C^1$ up to that boundary, with first derivatives $G_j$ there and their $C^{0,\alpha}$ bounds. This proves the last assertion under exactly Countable Choice. [step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be a disk or an upper half-disk in $\mathbb R^2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{2m}$ be open, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth, including the straight source boundary in the half-disk case, with $J^2=-I$. Let $u:G\to\Omega$ be continuous, belong locally to $W^{1,2}$, and satisfy
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$$
weakly. In the half-disk case assume continuity and local $W^{1,2}$ also up to the straight boundary, $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m\subset\mathbb C^m=\mathbb R^{2m}$, and $\mathbb R^m\cap J(s,0,u(s,0))\mathbb R^m=\{0\}$. Then $u$ is smooth locally, including all one-sided derivatives at the straight boundary. Thus a continuous $W^{1,2}$ weak solution in smooth target charts with a flattened totally real boundary has classical smooth regularity. Continuity at a missing puncture is a premise, not a conclusion.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The equation, local continuity and finite Sobolev norm, smooth coefficients, and totally real boundary condition in the statement.

[F1] Under Countable Choice, [[lem-countable-choice-lp-regularity-for-small-strip-cauchy-riemann-coefficients]] gives $W^{1,p}$ regularity and a derivative estimate for compactly supported $W^{1,2}$ solutions of $D_0w=A w_t+f$, with $\|A\|_\infty\le\eta_{m,p}$ and $f\in L^2\cap L^p$. It applies on the half-plane when $w$ is continuous with real boundary values, and applies locally by real cutoffs.

[F2] The actual Countable Choice proofs in [[thm-difference-quotient-characterisation-of-w-one-p-for-p-greater-than-one]] give uniform tangential quotient bounds from a weak tangential derivative, including on half-domains. Conversely, [[lem-weak-limit-of-uniformly-bounded-difference-quotients-is-the-weak-derivative]] turns such bounds into weak derivatives without weak compactness.

[F3] The Countable Choice proof in [[lem-countable-choice-planar-morrey-estimate]] gives local $W^{1,p}\subset C^{0,1-2/p}$ and $W^{2,p}\subset C^{1,1-2/p}$ for $p>2$, including straight boundaries.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 Work near one source point $z_0$. A constant real target change makes $J(z_0,u(z_0))=i$. At an interior point choose a real basis $e_1,Je_1,\ldots,e_m,Je_m$ successively in this finite-dimensional complex vector space. At a boundary point take a real basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ of the boundary plane; total reality makes $e_1,\ldots,e_m,Je_1,\ldots,Je_m$ a basis, and the change sending these vectors to the standard real and imaginary bases preserves the real boundary plane. Continuity of $u$ and smoothness of $J$ then give a disk or half-disk on which $$A(s,t)=i-J(s,t,u(s,t)),\qquad \|A\|_\infty<\min\{\eta_{m,8},\eta_{m,4}\}.$$ The equation becomes $D_0u=A u_t$. After further shrinking its image is in a compact subset of a convex target coordinate ball. All smooth coefficient derivatives are bounded there. Real cutoffs preserve the boundary condition. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 We record the weak calculus used below. For a continuous $W^{1,q}$ map, the chain rule $\partial_j H(z,u)=H_{z_j}(z,u)+H_x(z,u)\partial_j u$ holds for a smooth $H$ with bounded derivatives on its localized image. Indeed, on interior compact subsets mollify $u$: uniform convergence follows from continuity, convergence of derivatives holds in $L^q$, and the classical chain rule passes to distributions by boundedness and uniform convergence of the coefficient derivatives. This gives the formula everywhere in the open half-domain too; its bounds extend to the boundary because the formula has an integrable right side on the full half-domain. The product rule follows by the same argument whenever one factor and the relevant lower derivatives are bounded, or by Holder when the two differentiated factors have conjugate product integrability. Higher chain and product formulas follow inductively once the corresponding lower derivatives have these bounds. Difference quotients obey $\delta_s(fg)=f(s+h,t)\delta_s g+(\delta_s f)g$, and [F2] bounds the quotients by the weak derivatives on a slightly larger patch. These arguments use countably many mollifications and no selection of weakly convergent subsequences. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F1] with $p=8$ to a real-cutoff localization of $u$. Its forcing is $(\chi_s+i\chi_t-A\chi_t)u$, which is bounded and compactly supported because $u$ is continuous. The localized map is already $W^{1,2}$, and is continuous and real on the physical boundary. Thus $u\in W^{1,8}$ on a smaller patch. Step 2.1 implies $A\in W^{1,8}$ there. For each sufficiently small nonzero tangential shift $h$, put $v_h=\delta_su$ and $A_h(s,t)=A(s+h,t)$. Subtracting the equations gives $$D_0v_h=A_h(v_h)_t+(\delta_s A)u_t.$$ The last term has a uniform $L^4$ bound by Holder and [F2], since its factors have uniformly bounded $L^8$ norms. The local $L^4$ norm of $v_h$ is uniformly bounded by the tangential quotient estimate. Each $v_h$ separately is continuous, real on the boundary, and $W^{1,2}$: it is a difference of translates of a $W^{1,8}$ map divided by a fixed nonzero number. Therefore [F1] with $p=4$ and a fixed cutoff gives uniform $L^4$ bounds for $(v_h)_s,(v_h)_t$ on a still smaller patch; all forcing terms, including cutoff terms, lie in $L^4\cap L^2$ by finite support. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Apply the converse in [F2] to $u_s$ and $u_t$, whose tangential quotients are the uniformly bounded derivatives of $v_h$. It follows that $u_{ss},u_{st}\in L^4$. The original equation equivalently says $u_t=J(s,t,u)u_s$, since $J^2=-I$. Differentiate this weakly in $t$ using step 2.1: $$u_{tt}=(J_t+J_xu_t)u_s+J u_{st}.$$ Here $J_t$ denotes its explicit source derivative. Both first derivatives of $u$ are in $L^8$, so the product term lies in $L^4$; the other terms do too. Thus $u\in W^{2,4}$ locally. By [F3], $u$ is now $C^{1,1/2}$ on smaller patches up to the physical boundary, with bounded first derivatives. In particular its classical tangential boundary derivative is real. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Suppose inductively $u\in W^{k,4}$ locally for an integer $k\ge2$. By [F3] applied to its derivatives of order at most $k-2$, all derivatives of order at most $k-1$ have continuous bounded representatives on smaller patches. Repeated use of step 2.1 gives $A\in W^{k,4}$, with all its derivatives of order at most $k-1$ bounded. Put $v=\partial_s^{k-1}u$. Its differentiated equation is $$D_0v=A v_t+G,\qquad G=\sum_{a=1}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{a}(\partial_s^a A)(\partial_t\partial_s^{k-1-a}u).$$ The function $G$ and its weak $s$ derivative lie in $L^4$: in a differentiated product at most one factor has order $k$, which is $L^4$; every other factor has order at most $k-1$ and is bounded. The same reasoning applies to the chain expansion for $A$, since a term containing a derivative of order $k$ contains it only once. The function $v$ is continuous, belongs to $W^{1,4}$, and has real boundary values, being the tangential derivative of order $k-1$ of a $C^{k-1}$ map whose boundary trace is real. [F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Take tangential quotients of the last equation: $$D_0(\delta_s v)=A_h\partial_t(\delta_s v)+(\delta_s A)v_t+\delta_sG.$$ The quotient forcing is uniformly $L^4$ on smaller patches: $\delta_sA$ is uniformly bounded by the bounded classical first derivative of $A$, $v_t\in L^4$, and $\delta_sG$ is controlled by $G_s\in L^4$ and [F2]. Also $\delta_s v$ is uniformly $L^4$ by $v_s\in L^4$. For each fixed $h$ it is continuous, real on the boundary, and $W^{1,2}$ on bounded patches, so [F1] and cutoffs give uniform $L^4$ bounds for its first derivatives. The converse in [F2] gives $\partial_s^{k+1}u,\partial_t\partial_s^k u\in L^4$. This supplies the derivatives of total order $k+1$ with zero or one normal derivative. [F1, F2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Recover the other derivatives from $u_t=Ju_s$. For a derivative of total order $k+1$ with $b\ge2$ normal derivatives, apply $\partial_s^{k+1-b}\partial_t^{b-1}$ to this equation. The term in which no derivative hits $J$ is $J\partial_s^{k+2-b}\partial_t^{b-1}u$, already known by induction on $b$. In every other product, derivatives of $u$ have order at most $k$, and differentiated coefficient factors have order at most $k$. If a factor has order $k$, it is the only such factor and all others are bounded; otherwise all factors are bounded. Thus all these terms lie in $L^4$ on a bounded smaller patch. For precision, first differentiate the equation only $k-1$ times, by $\partial_s^{k+1-b}\partial_t^{b-2}$, and then take one more weak $t$ derivative. The highest differentiated $u_s$ factor has a known weak $t$ derivative by the induction on $b$; its coefficient $J$ is $C^1$, so the ordinary first-order weak product rule applies. All other factors have the bounded or $L^4$ derivatives just described. This justifies the displayed expansion without multiplying an undefined high-order distribution by a nonsmooth coefficient, and proves the desired derivative exists in $L^4$. Induction on $b$ proves $u\in W^{k+1,4}$. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Starting with step 4.1, steps 5.1 through 7.1 prove local $W^{k,4}$ for every finite $k$, using nested patches inside the original coordinate neighborhood. To obtain a fixed neighborhood for any specified order, choose its finitely many nested patches between that neighborhood and a larger one; no uniform positive loss after infinitely many inductions is needed. Applying [F3] to each derivative then gives classical derivatives of every order, with their continuous extensions to the straight boundary and the usual tangential boundary derivatives. The given continuous representative agrees with each Sobolev representative. The equation therefore holds classically and $u$ is smooth as asserted. This conclusion requires the initial continuity premise and does not establish it at any puncture. [F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,g)$ be a compact smooth manifold and let $J(z,x)$ be a smooth family of almost complex structures for $z$ in a disk about $0$, smooth also at $z=0$. A smooth solution $u_s+J(z,u)u_t=0$ on the punctured disk with finite Dirichlet energy extends smoothly over $0$.

The same holds on a punctured upper half-disk with boundary on a fixed compact totally real submanifold $L\subset X$, provided $J(z,x)=J(0,x)$ for $x\in L$ and real $z$ near $0$. Smoothness and the boundary condition of $u$ are assumed up to the two open straight boundary intervals. The extension is smooth up to the filled boundary point and remains on $L$ there.

In particular, for autonomous $J(x)$, every finite-energy smooth plane map extends over infinity to a smooth $J$-holomorphic sphere, and every finite-energy smooth upper-half-plane map with compact totally real boundary extends over infinity to a smooth disk. No bubble-tree, energy identity for a sequence, or gluing statement is included.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The compact smooth target, smooth almost complex family, punctured-domain solution, finite energy, and, when present, the fixed totally real boundary data in the statement.

[F1] The actual interior and totally real boundary small-energy derivative estimates are [[lem-interior-energy-regularity-for-smooth-almost-complex-strips]] and [[lem-boundary-energy-regularity-for-totally-real-strips]]. The latter requires the boundary complex structure restricted to $L$ to be independent of its tangential source coordinate, as stipulated here.

[F2] A continuous weak $W^{1,2}$ solution is smooth in local charts, including a flattened totally real boundary, by [[lem-continuous-weak-almost-complex-strip-solutions-are-smooth]].

[F3] The finite-dimensional smooth inverse results used below have actual proofs in [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] and [[thm-higher-regularity-of-local-inverses]].

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 We first construct convenient finite-dimensional target data. Take finitely many coordinate charts $U_i$ and smaller relatively compact chart neighborhoods covering $X$. Euclidean smooth bumps supported in $U_i$, equal to one on those smaller neighborhoods, normalized by their positive sum, give a finite smooth partition $\phi_i$. The map $$F:X\longrightarrow\mathbb R^N,\qquad F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$$ is smooth, interpreting each coordinate product as zero off its compact support. It is injective: if $F(x)=F(y)$ choose $i$ with $\phi_i(x)>0$; the equal first coordinates and coordinate products give $x_i(x)=x_i(y)$. Its derivative is injective by the same argument: if $dF(v)=0$, then $d\phi_i(v)=0$ for all $i$, and at such an $i$ the product derivative gives $\phi_i dx_i(v)=0$. Compactness makes $F$ a homeomorphism onto its image, and [F3] in local coordinates gives smooth inverse charts on that image. Thus $F$ is a smooth embedding. Its induced derivative norms are uniformly equivalent to the original metric norms. No general embedding theorem is needed. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Use cylindrical coordinates $z=-e^{-\sigma-i\tau}$ about the puncture and put $v(\sigma,\tau)=u(-e^{-\sigma-i\tau})$. The angular variable has period $2\pi$ in the interior case and lies in $[0,\pi]$ in the boundary case. This holomorphic coordinate change preserves the equation and Dirichlet energy: $$v_\sigma+J(-e^{-\sigma-i\tau},v)v_\tau=0,\qquad \int_{\sigma>S}(|v_\sigma|_g^2+|v_\tau|_g^2)<\infty,$$ with that tail integral tending to zero as $S\to\infty$. The composed coefficients have uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order; positive cylindrical source derivatives of $-e^{-\sigma-i\tau}$ are bounded and tend to zero. Their restriction to $L$ on the two physical boundary edges is the fixed structure $J(0,x)$, so [F1] applies uniformly on fixed-radius cylinder disks or boundary half-disks. Choose their radius smaller than $\pi/8$. Every point is covered by an interior estimate or a boundary half-radius estimate on such a patch. For sufficiently large $S$ the patch energies are below the fixed threshold, and [F1] gives $$\sup_{\tau}|dv(\sigma,\tau)|_g\longrightarrow0\quad(\sigma\to\infty).$$ This argument uses target-global estimates and assumes no prior containment in one target chart. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write $Y=F(X)$ and $P_x=dF_x$. Relative to $g$ and the Euclidean metric the map $Q_x=(P_x^*P_x)^{-1}P_x^*$ is a smooth left inverse of $P_x$. Define on $Y$ the smooth ambient operator $$K(z,F(x))=P_xJ(z,x)Q_x.$$ For $U=F\circ u$, the equation is $U_s+K(z,U)U_t=0$. These operators are uniformly bounded and Lipschitz in their $Y$ variable for $z$ near zero. To justify the global Lipschitz bound, on each of finitely many smaller image charts, bounded coordinate derivatives and the local inverse estimates bound operator differences by Euclidean chord length. All sufficiently close pairs of points lie in one such chart, by compactness and the Lebesgue-number property of a finite cover. For pairs whose distance is bounded below, boundedness of $K$ gives the same Lipschitz inequality after enlarging the constant. Also $|K(z,a)-K(0,a)|\le C|z|$ uniformly for $a\in Y$, by bounded source derivatives. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 For use in the boundary case we construct an ambient retraction $R$ from a neighborhood of $F(L)$ to $F(L)$ such that $$dR_{F(x)}\bigl(P_xJ(0,x)v\bigr)=0\qquad(v\in T_xL).$$ In the Euclidean ambient space let $$N_x=P_xJ(0,x)T_xL\oplus(P_xT_xX)^\perp.$$ Total reality makes $\mathbb R^N=P_xT_xL\oplus N_x$. In finite local frames of this smooth vector bundle, the derivative at $(x,0)$ of $\Psi(x,v)=F(x)+v$ is an isomorphism, so [F3] supplies smooth local inverses. The map is injective on $|v|<\delta$ for some uniform $\delta>0$. Otherwise choose collisions with both normal vectors tending to zero; compactness gives a subsequence of their base points converging, equality of the images forces the two limits equal, and the local inverse near that zero-section point contradicts the collisions. Its derivative remains invertible on a smaller uniform neighborhood by the same compactness argument. Consequently its image is an open neighborhood of $F(L)$, its local inverses agree, and projection to the base defines the claimed smooth retraction $R$. On a still smaller neighborhood its first two derivatives are bounded. The projection differential is the identity on $P_xT_xL$ and zero on $N_x$, proving the displayed property. [F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.3 Set $V=F\circ v$, and define $$e(\sigma)=\int_I|V_\tau(\sigma,\tau)|^2d\tau,\qquad b(\sigma)=\frac1{|I|}\int_I V(\sigma,\tau)d\tau,$$ where $I$ is one angular period or $[0,\pi]$. Then $\int_S^\infty e(\sigma)d\sigma<\infty$, $e(\sigma)\to0$, and $$\sup_\tau|V(\sigma,\tau)-b(\sigma)|\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}\longrightarrow0.$$ The last estimate follows from the fundamental theorem on the angular interval, Holder, and averaging. In particular every angular slice has vanishing diameter. The map $b$ is smooth for finite $\sigma$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 There is also a uniform quadratic chord estimate: for $a,a'\in F(L)$ sufficiently close, $$|dR_a K(0,a)(a'-a)|\le C|a'-a|^2.$$ Indeed choose a local smooth parametrization $\ell$ of $F(L)$ about $a$. Taylor's formula gives $a'-a=d\ell\,h+O(|h|^2)$ and the local inverse estimate gives $|h|\le C|a'-a|$. The operator $K(0,a)$ sends the first tangent term into $P_xJ(0,x)T_xL$, killed by $dR_a$ from step 2.2. Bounded second derivatives give the remainder estimate, uniformly by a finite cover. The same finite-cover argument gives $|dR_b-dR_a|\le C|b-a|$ when $a\in F(L)$ and $b$ is sufficiently close to $a$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

3.2 In the interior case choose $a=V(\sigma,0)$ and $K_0=K(0,a)$. Periodicity gives $\int_I V_\tau=0$. Therefore the equation and step 2.1 imply $$|b'(\sigma)|=\left|\frac1{|I|}\int_I(K_0-K(-e^{-\sigma-i\tau},V))V_\tau d\tau\right|\le C e(\sigma)+C e^{-\sigma}\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ The right side is integrable: the first term by finite energy and the second by Holder against $e^{-\sigma}$. Thus $b$ has finite total variation on the infinite tail, hence has a Euclidean limit. Step 2.3 shows all $V(\sigma,\tau)$ approach that same limit uniformly in $\tau$. Since $Y$ is compact and closed, the limit lies in $Y$. [step 2.1, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 In the boundary case $a=V(\sigma,0)$ and $a'=V(\sigma,\pi)$ lie in $F(L)$. For large $\sigma$, step 2.3 puts $b(\sigma)$ in the neighborhood of the retraction $R$. The same calculation now gives $$b'=-\frac1\pi K(0,a)(a'-a)+q,\qquad |q|\le C e(\sigma)+C e^{-\sigma}\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ Let $c(\sigma)=R(b(\sigma))\in F(L)$. By step 3.1 and $|a'-a|+|b-a|\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}$, $$|dR_bK(0,a)(a'-a)|\le C\bigl(|a'-a|^2+|b-a|\,|a'-a|\bigr)\le C e(\sigma).$$ Boundedness of $dR$ therefore gives the same integrable bound for $|c'|$. Thus $c(\sigma)$ converges to a point of compact $F(L)$. Moreover $|b-c|\le C|b-a|\to0$, since $R(a)=a$, and step 2.3 proves that every $V(\sigma,\tau)$ converges uniformly to that same point. The endpoint contribution has been estimated quadratically, rather than discarded. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 2.3, algebra]

5.1 By the inverse homeomorphism of $F$, steps 3.2 and 4.1 give a unique continuous extension of $u$ to the puncture, with value on $L$ in the boundary case. Localize now in a smooth target chart about that limiting value; in the boundary case use any smooth submanifold chart flattening $L$ to $\mathbb R^m$. The transformed map is continuous and has square-integrable first derivatives off zero. It belongs to $W^{1,2}$ across zero. For the interior assertion, multiply a compact test by a radial cutoff vanishing on radius $\varepsilon$ and equal to one outside radius $2\varepsilon$. In integration by parts the cutoff-error term is at most $C\|u\|_\infty\|\varphi\|_\infty\varepsilon$, since the cutoff gradient has $L^1$ norm $O(\varepsilon)$. All other terms converge by integrability. This proves the weak derivative identity on the whole disk with the original $L^2$ derivative. On a half-disk the identical cutoff argument works, or one can note that zero lies on its physical boundary and the weak identities in its open interior are already available with finite $L^2$ norm up to that edge. The equation holds almost everywhere and hence weakly after filling the measure-zero point. [step 1.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 The coordinate chain rule needed in step 5.1 follows by smooth mollification on smaller patches: continuity gives uniform convergence of coefficient compositions and the weak derivatives converge in $L^2$, so the classical smooth chain rule passes to distributions. Thus the transformed coefficients remain smooth, the boundary plane remains totally real, and all hypotheses of [F2] hold. That lemma proves a smooth extension, including the boundary case. Its boundary value lies in $L$ by step 4.1. The extension adds no energy, since its new point has measure zero. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Finally, for an autonomous plane solution use the holomorphic coordinate $z=1/w$ at infinity; conformal invariance preserves finite energy and produces a punctured-disk solution of the same autonomous equation. The proved interior assertion fills it and gives a sphere map. For an upper-half-plane solution use $z=-1/w$, which preserves the upper half-plane and its real boundary; the boundary assertion fills infinity. The upper half-plane together with that point is smoothly conformally a closed disk, as is seen explicitly by a Mobius map from the half-plane to the disk. All other finite boundary points were already smooth. These are statements about one finite-energy map; they do not infer compactification, no-neck convergence, or gluing for a sequence. [step 1.2, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix a compact smooth Riemannian manifold $(X,g)$ and a period $T>0$. Consider smooth families $J(\sigma,\tau,x)^2=-I$ on cylinders $[a,b]\times(\mathbb R/T\mathbb Z)$, with uniform bounds for $J$ and its first two target covariant derivatives. There are constants $\varepsilon,c,C>0$ depending only on these data such that the following holds. If
$$u_\sigma+J(\sigma,\tau,u)u_\tau=0,\qquad \sup|du|_g+\sup(|\partial_\sigma J|+|\partial_\tau J|)\le\varepsilon,$$
then a fixed smooth embedding $F:X\to\mathbb R^N$ can be chosen once for the target so that, for $V=F\circ u$ and $e(\sigma)=\tfrac12\int_0^T|V_\tau|^2d\tau$,
$$e''\ge c^2 e,\qquad e(\sigma)\le e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}.$$
Consequently, for $0\le R\le(b-a)/2$,
$$E_g\bigl(u;[a+R,b-R]\times S_T^1\bigr)\le C(e(a)+e(b))e^{-cR}.$$
Here $E_g=\tfrac12\int|du|_g^2$. The energy density at either endpoint is bounded by $CT\varepsilon^2$. Thus central neck energies tend to zero as $R\to\infty$, uniformly in neck length, for maps satisfying these hypotheses. This statement concerns closed cylinders, not boundary necks.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The compact target, uniform coefficient bounds, fixed angular period, equation, and smallness hypotheses of the statement.

[F1] The direct covariant computation in [[lem-interior-energy-regularity-for-smooth-almost-complex-strips]] proves, writing $q=u_\sigma$, $$\nabla_\sigma u_\sigma+\nabla_\tau u_\tau=(\nabla_{Jq}J)q+J(\nabla_qJ)q+(\partial_\tau J+J\partial_\sigma J)q.$$ In particular its norm is at most $C|du|_g^2+C\kappa|du|_g$, where $\kappa=\sup(|\partial_\sigma J|+|\partial_\tau J|)$ denotes only explicit source derivatives.

[F2] The Countable Choice proof of [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]] gives periodic Wirtinger: for a smooth mean-zero vector-valued periodic $w$, $\int_0^T|w_\tau|^2\ge(2\pi/T)^2\int_0^T|w|^2$, by applying Parseval componentwise and observing that the zero Fourier coefficient vanishes.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 Choose a finite chart cover and smooth subordinate functions $\phi_i$ with compact supports in those charts and sum one, obtained by Euclidean bumps and normalization. The map $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$ is a smooth embedding: at an index where $\phi_i>0$, equality of the displayed coordinates recovers the original chart point, and vanishing of all their derivatives recovers a zero tangent vector. Compactness makes it a homeomorphism onto its image and makes its differential uniformly comparable with the metric $g$. Its first and second covariant derivatives have uniform bounds. This fixes $F$ independently of the cylinder and its map. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $H=\Delta V$, taking the ordinary flat source Laplacian componentwise. The composition rule and [F1] give $$H=dF(\nabla_\sigma u_\sigma+\nabla_\tau u_\tau)+(\nabla dF)(u_\sigma,u_\sigma)+(\nabla dF)(u_\tau,u_\tau).$$ Uniform coefficient and embedding bounds therefore give $|H|\le C_0(|du|_g+\kappa)|du|_g$. The original equation and the bound for $J$ give $|du|_g\le C_1|u_\tau|_g\le C_2|V_\tau|$. After imposing the stated smallness, $$|H|\le C_3\varepsilon|V_\tau|.$$ This is a pointwise estimate on actual maps into $X$; no ambient extension of $J$ or model moduli equation is assumed. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Put $w=V_\tau$. It has zero angular mean because $V$ is periodic, and $\Delta w=\partial_\tau H$ because derivatives of a smooth Euclidean map commute. Twice differentiating $e=\tfrac12\int|w|^2$ and integrating by parts only in the periodic angular direction gives $$e''=\int_0^T\bigl(|w_\sigma|^2+|w_\tau|^2-\langle w_\tau,H\rangle\bigr)d\tau.$$ There are no endpoint terms in this integration. By step 2.1 and Young's inequality this is at least $$\int_0^T|w_\sigma|^2+\tfrac12|w_\tau|^2-\tfrac12 C_3^2\varepsilon^2|w|^2\,d\tau.$$ Let $\lambda=(2\pi/T)^2$ and choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that $C_3^2\varepsilon^2\le\lambda/2$. Then [F2] gives $e''\ge(\lambda/4)\int|w|^2=(\lambda/2)e$. Set $c=\sqrt{\lambda/2}$. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Let $h(\sigma)=e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}$. It satisfies $h''-c^2h=0$ and dominates $e$ at both endpoints. If $e-h$ had a positive value, it would have a positive interior maximum; there its second derivative is nonpositive, contrary to $(e-h)''\ge c^2(e-h)>0$. Thus $e\le h$ throughout the cylinder, giving the claimed pointwise exponential bound. The argument also covers vanishing endpoint values, since $e$ is nonnegative and smooth. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The equation and uniform metric comparability give $$E_g(u;[a+R,b-R]\times S_T^1)\le C_4\int_{a+R}^{b-R}e(\sigma)d\sigma.$$ Integrating the two exponentials from step 4.1 bounds the last integral by $c^{-1}(e(a)+e(b))e^{-cR}$. Finally $|V_\tau|\le C|u_\tau|_g\le C\varepsilon$, so $e(a)+e(b)\le CT\varepsilon^2$. This proves all assertions, including uniform decay of central neck energy. A boundary neck has angular endpoint terms and is not covered by the periodic argument. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix a compact smooth Riemannian target $(X,g)$, a compact half-dimensional submanifold $L$, a smooth complex structure $J_b$ on $TX|_L$ for which $L$ is totally real, and an angular length $T>0$. Let $J(\sigma,\tau,x)$ be smooth almost complex structures on $[a,b]\times[0,T]\times X$, with uniform bounds for $J$ and its first two target covariant derivatives, and with $J(\sigma,0,x)=J(\sigma,T,x)=J_b(x)$ for $x\in L$. There are constants $\varepsilon,c,C>0$, independent of $a,b$, such that every smooth solution
$$u_\sigma+J(\sigma,\tau,u)u_\tau=0,\qquad u(\sigma,0),u(\sigma,T)\in L,$$
with $\sup|du|_g+\sup(|\partial_\sigma J|+|\partial_\tau J|)\le\varepsilon$ satisfies
$$E_g(u;[a+R,b-R]\times[0,T])\le C\varepsilon^2e^{-cR}\qquad(0\le R\le(b-a)/2).$$
In particular central energies vanish uniformly with the distance $R$ from the ends of these long boundary necks. Both angular edges lie on the same $L$; this is not a statement about strips with two different boundary submanifolds.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The compact geometric data, uniform bounds, fixed boundary complex structure, actual equation, and small-gradient and source-variation bounds of the statement.

[F1] The covariant tension identity proved in [[lem-interior-energy-regularity-for-smooth-almost-complex-strips]] bounds the target tension of such a solution by $C(|du|_g^2+\kappa|du|_g)$, where $\kappa$ is the bound for explicit source derivatives of $J$.

[F2] The actual Countable Choice proof of [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]] gives periodic Wirtinger, $\int_0^{2T}|w_\tau|^2\ge(\pi/T)^2\int_0^{2T}|w|^2$ when $w$ has zero mean.

[F3] Smooth local inverses used here are supplied by the actual proofs in [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] and [[thm-higher-regularity-of-local-inverses]].

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 A fixed finite-atlas embedding is obtained as follows. Choose a finite smooth partition $\phi_i$ with compact supports in coordinate charts $x_i$, using finite Euclidean bumps and normalization, and set $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$. Equality of these coordinates recovers $x$ in a chart where $\phi_i>0$, and vanishing of their derivatives recovers a zero tangent vector in that chart. Thus $F$ is injective and immersive, and compactness makes it an embedding. Derivatives of $F$ are bounded and its differential uniformly compares $g$ with the ambient Euclidean metric. Write $Y=F(X)$ and $M=F(L)$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 We construct a smooth involution $\rho$ on a neighborhood of $L$ in $X$, fixing $L$, whose differential is $+I$ on $TL$ and $-I$ on $J_bTL$. First the ambient normal map $(y,n)\mapsto y+n$ from the Euclidean orthogonal normal bundle of $Y$ has invertible differential along its zero section. By [F3] it has local smooth inverses. It is injective for a uniform small normal radius: otherwise collisions with normal vectors tending to zero have base points converging after a subsequence by compactness; equality of images forces the same base limit, contradicting the local inverse there. The same compactness argument preserves invertible differential on a uniform radius. Projection of these glued inverses to $Y$ gives a smooth ambient retraction $P$ near $Y$ with $dP$ the tangent projection along $Y$. Now on the vector bundle $N_y=dF(J_bT_xL)$ over $y=F(x)\in M$, consider $\Phi(y,v)=P(y+v)\in Y$. At $v=0$ its derivative identifies $T_yM\oplus N_y$ with $T_yY$, since $L$ is totally real. The identical local-inverse and compactness argument gives a diffeomorphism from a uniform small symmetric bundle neighborhood onto a neighborhood of $M$ in $Y$. Conjugating $(y,v)\mapsto(y,-v)$ by this diffeomorphism and then by $F$ defines $\rho$. It is an involution, fixes $L$, and has the claimed differential. On a smaller fixed neighborhood all its first and second derivatives, and its inverse differential, are bounded. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For small enough $\varepsilon$, the entire map lies in that fixed neighborhood: each path $\tau\mapsto u(\sigma,\tau)$ begins on $L$ and has length at most $T\varepsilon$. Define on the doubled angular circle of period $2T$ $$\widetilde u(\sigma,\tau)=\begin{cases}u(\sigma,\tau),&0\le\tau\le T,\\ \rho(u(\sigma,-\tau)),&-T\le\tau\le0,\end{cases}$$ identifying $-T$ and $T$. This is $C^1$ across both seams. Values agree because $\rho$ fixes $L$. Tangential derivatives agree because $u_\sigma\in TL$ there, so $d\rho u_\sigma=u_\sigma$. The equation gives $u_\tau=J_bu_\sigma\in J_bTL$, so the normal reflected derivative $-d\rho u_\tau$ equals $u_\tau$. These identities hold along the whole seam and may also be differentiated in $\sigma$. Thus all tangential derivatives of the values and normal first derivatives match. The doubled map is smooth on each closed side. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Put $V=F\circ\widetilde u$ and let $H=\Delta V$ weakly on the doubled cylinder. There is no line measure in this Laplacian because $V$ and its first derivatives match across the seams; integrating by parts on both sides verifies cancellation. On the original half, the composition formula and [F1] bound $|H|\le C(|du|_g^2+\kappa|du|_g)$. On the reflected half the composition rule for $F\circ\rho$ gives the same bound, with a larger fixed constant from its second derivatives. The equation gives $|du|_g\le C|u_\tau|_g$, and the embedding and reflected inverse differential compare this with $|V_\tau|$ on either side. Hence $$|H|\le C_0\varepsilon|V_\tau|$$ almost everywhere on the entire doubled cylinder. This argument does not assume a globally smooth reflected almost complex coefficient across a seam. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Set $w=V_\tau$ and $e(\sigma)=\tfrac12\int_{-T}^T|w|^2d\tau$. The function $w$ is continuous and piecewise smooth, its angular derivative is an ordinary bounded piecewise function locally, and it has zero angular mean. Moreover $\Delta w=\partial_\tau H$ as distributions. Tangential differentiation of the piecewise formulas gives $$e''=\int_{-T}^T\bigl(|w_\sigma|^2+|w_\tau|^2-\langle w_\tau,H\rangle\bigr)d\tau.$$ For completeness the last integration by parts is distributional: $w$ is periodic $H^1$ in its angular variable and $H\in L^2$, so convolution on that circle proves $\langle\partial_\tau H,w\rangle=-\int\langle H,w_\tau\rangle$ by passage to the $L^2$ limit. Thus any jumps of $H$ are included, and no angular endpoint term was omitted. The matching tangential derivatives from step 3.1 justify differentiating the integral twice in $\sigma$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Young's inequality and [F2] give, for $\lambda=(\pi/T)^2$, $$e''\ge\tfrac12\int|w_\tau|^2-\tfrac12C_0^2\varepsilon^2\int|w|^2\ge\tfrac12(\lambda-C_0^2\varepsilon^2)\int|w|^2.$$ Decrease $\varepsilon$ so that $C_0^2\varepsilon^2\le\lambda/2$ and set $c=\sqrt{\lambda/2}$. Then $e''\ge c^2e$. The barrier $h=e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}$ has $h''=c^2h$ and dominates the endpoint values of $e$. A positive interior maximum of $e-h$ would contradict $(e-h)''\ge c^2(e-h)$, so $e\le h$. Its integral on $[a+R,b-R]$ is at most $c^{-1}(e(a)+e(b))e^{-cR}$. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 The original energy is bounded by $C\int e(\sigma)d\sigma$, by the original equation and embedding norm equivalence. The small derivative hypothesis and the fixed reflected derivative bound give $e(a)+e(b)\le C\varepsilon^2$. Substitution in step 6.1 proves the asserted central energy estimate with a uniform constant. This proves boundary neck decay using the actual totally real boundary geometry. It does not address two different submanifolds or construct a bubble-tree decomposition. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix compact target and coefficient bounds as in the interior and boundary cylinder-neck lemmas. Let $D$ be either an angular circle of fixed length $T$, or the interval $[0,T]$ with both edges on the same fixed compact totally real $L$ and with fixed boundary structure $J_b$. Coefficient bounds include uniform $C^2$ bounds in source and target, and, in the boundary case, $J(\sigma,0,x)=J(\sigma,T,x)=J_b(x)$ for $x\in L$.

There are constants $\delta_0,\kappa_0,c,C>0$ depending only on these data such that the following holds. Let $u$ be a smooth actual almost complex solution on $[a-1,b+1]\times D$, with explicit source derivatives of $J$ bounded by $\kappa_0$. Suppose $0<\delta\le\delta_0$ and every source disk or physical-boundary half-disk of one fixed radius $r_0<\min\{1/8,T/16\}$, contained in this cylinder, has energy at most $\delta$. Then for $0\le R\le(b-a)/2$,
$$E_g(u;[a+R,b-R]\times D)\le C\delta e^{-cR},$$
and
$$\operatorname{diam}_g u([a+R,b-R]\times D)\le C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2}.$$
In particular, for any sequence of such necks, their central energy and image diameter tend uniformly to zero as their distance $R$ from the ends tends to infinity. This is a criterion for a neck already satisfying the stated local-energy bound; no bubble-tree decomposition is assumed or asserted.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The actual smooth solution and local-energy hypotheses, fixed angular geometry, compact target, coefficient bounds, and boundary data in the statement.

[F1] [[lem-interior-energy-regularity-for-smooth-almost-complex-strips]] and [[lem-boundary-energy-regularity-for-totally-real-strips]] give target-global gradient bounds on smaller fixed-radius patches from sufficiently small energy; the boundary statement requires the fixed $J_b$ stipulated here.

[F2] The actual proofs of [[lem-small-gradient-almost-complex-cylinder-neck-energy-decay]] and [[lem-small-gradient-totally-real-boundary-neck-energy-decay]] construct a fixed target embedding $F$ and, for boundary necks, a fixed smooth reflection $\rho$ about $L$. For the embedded original periodic map, or its $C^1$ periodic double, they prove $$e(\sigma)=\tfrac12\int|V_\tau|^2,\qquad e''\ge c^2e,\qquad e(\sigma)\le e(a)e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e(b)e^{-c(b-\sigma)}$$ once gradients and explicit source variations are sufficiently small. They also prove the original energy is at most $C\int e$, with constants independent of cylinder length. The constructions and estimates are part of those explicit proofs, not assumptions about a moduli space.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 Fix the patch radius $r_0$ in the statement, decreasing it if necessary to satisfy the uniform scale restrictions of [F1]. Every point in $[a,b]\times D$ is covered by an interior smaller patch or a boundary half-radius patch of this radius, contained in the extended cylinder. In the angular interval case, points within $r_0/4$ of an edge use the boundary supremum estimate centered at their boundary foot; other points use an interior disk of radius at least $r_0/8$. Their energies are at most $\delta$: if their radii are smaller, each is contained in one stipulated radius-$r_0$ patch. In the angular circle case all points use an interior disk. Choosing $\delta_0$ below the [F1] thresholds gives $$\sup_{[a,b]\times D}|du|_g\le C_0\sqrt\delta.$$ The unit buffer ensures these patches remain in the prescribed source domain even at $\sigma=a,b$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose $\delta_0$ further so that $C_0\sqrt{\delta_0}$ is below half the small-gradient threshold in [F2], and choose $\kappa_0$ below half its source-variation threshold. All hypotheses of the corresponding neck estimate hold on $[a,b]\times D$. In the boundary case the small derivative bound also places every angular half-loop in the fixed reflection collar, since it starts on $L$ and has length at most $TC_0\sqrt\delta$. Thus the original periodic embedding, or the reflected periodic double in [F2], is genuinely defined. Its angular period is $T$ or $2T$, and its endpoint slice energies obey $e(a)+e(b)\le C_1\delta$, by the derivative estimate in step 1.1 and the fixed differential bounds of $F$ and $\rho$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The exponential barrier in [F2] therefore gives $$e(\sigma)\le C_1\delta\bigl(e^{-c(\sigma-a)}+e^{-c(b-\sigma)}\bigr).$$ Its integral on the central interval is at most $C\delta e^{-cR}$, proving the asserted energy bound. The same inequality and $\sqrt{x+y}\le\sqrt x+\sqrt y$ give $$\int_{a+R}^{b-R}\sqrt{e(\sigma)}d\sigma\le C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2},\qquad \sup_{[a+R,b-R]}\sqrt e\le C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2}.$$ These bounds do not multiply by cylinder length, since the exponential tails are integrated explicitly. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $P$ be the fixed angular period of $V$, and $B(\sigma)=P^{-1}\int V(\sigma,\tau)d\tau$. Angular integration and Holder give $$|V(\sigma,\tau)-B(\sigma)|\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ Moreover $|V_\sigma|\le C|V_\tau|$ on each side, by the original equation, bounded $J$, and the fixed reflection differential and its inverse. Thus $$|B'(\sigma)|\le P^{-1}\int|V_\sigma|d\tau\le C\sqrt{e(\sigma)}.$$ For any two central source points, compare their embedded values to their slice averages and integrate this bound for $B'$ between the slices. Step 3.1 proves that the Euclidean diameter of their embedded images is at most $C\sqrt\delta e^{-cR/2}$. This uses no cancellation of angular endpoint terms; the reflected periodic map is used only after its actual construction in [F2]. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Finally the inverse of the fixed compact embedding is uniformly locally Lipschitz in ambient chord distance. Indeed in each smaller image chart its inverse derivative is bounded; compactness gives a uniform closeness scale within one chart. For pairs separated by more than that scale, the diameter of each relevant compact target component enlarges the constant to a global bound. The connected image of our cylinder lies in one target component, and a compact manifold has finitely many components. Consequently $d_g(x,y)\le C|F(x)-F(y)|$ for pairs in that component, with uniform constant. Applying this to step 4.1 gives the asserted target diameter estimate. Hence both energy and image collapse with $R$ as claimed, conditional only on the concrete local-energy and source-variation bounds in the statement. [step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,g)$ be compact, let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact smooth half-dimensional submanifolds with finite intersection, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth almost complex structures on $[0,\infty)\times[0,1]\times X$ with uniform $C^2$ bounds in source and target. Assume $J(s,j,x)=J_{b,j}(x)$ for $x\in L_j$, independent of $s$, and that $L_j$ is totally real for $J_{b,j}$. A smooth solution
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0,\qquad u(s,j)\in L_j,$$
with finite Dirichlet energy has a unique point $x_+\in L_0\cap L_1$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le1}d_g(u(s,t),x_+)\longrightarrow0,\qquad \sup_{0\le t\le1}|du(s,t)|_g\longrightarrow0$$
as $s\to\infty$. In particular no such strip exists if $L_0\cap L_1$ is empty. Compact transverse half-dimensional $L_0,L_1$ satisfy the finite-intersection premise. The analogous conclusion holds at a negative strip end. No exponential rate or index theorem is asserted.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The actual smooth half-strip, compact target and boundary submanifolds, coefficient bounds, fixed boundary structures, and finite energy from the statement.

[F1] The proved target-global interior and boundary epsilon estimates are [[lem-interior-energy-regularity-for-smooth-almost-complex-strips]] and [[lem-boundary-energy-regularity-for-totally-real-strips]]. Their constants are uniform under the stipulated coefficient bounds; the boundary structures are fixed in $s$ exactly as required there.

[F2] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] gives local coordinates in which two transverse complementary-dimensional submanifolds have isolated intersection, by applying the theorem to the difference of their local parametrizations.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 Choose a fixed radius $r>0$ less than $1/16$ and the uniform scale restrictions in [F1]. Since the total energy is finite, the tail energy $E(u;[S,\infty)\times[0,1])$ tends to zero. Each point $(s,t)$ with $s>S+1$ is covered by an interior smaller disk or a boundary half-radius patch of fixed radius comparable to $r$, contained in that tail. Points within $r/4$ of a physical edge use the boundary supremum estimate centered at their boundary foot; other points use a fixed smaller interior disk. At the upper edge the orientation-preserving coordinate $(s,t)\mapsto(-s,1-t)$ turns it into a lower half-plane edge and preserves the equation, replacing the source arguments in $J$ only; its boundary structure is still fixed. Thus [F1] applies with uniform constants on every such patch. Once the tail energy is below its threshold, $$\sup_{s>S+1,\,0\le t\le1}|du(s,t)|_g^2\le C E(u;[S,\infty)\times[0,1]).$$ The right side tends to zero. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The angular slice length is at most $\sup_t|u_t(s,t)|_g$, so step 1.1 implies $$\sup_t d_g(u(s,t),u(s,0))\longrightarrow0.$$ Any sequence $s_n\to\infty$ has a subsequence for which $u(s_n,0)$ converges, by compactness of $X$. Its limit lies in closed $L_0$. Since $u(s_n,1)\in L_1$ and their mutual distances tend to zero, the same limit lies in closed $L_1$. Consequently the distance from the entire tail image to $L_0\cap L_1$ tends to zero. Indeed, otherwise choose a sequence of image points with distance bounded below; compactness and the vanishing slice diameter would produce a subsequential limit in the intersection, a contradiction. If the intersection were empty the very first subsequence argument would already contradict that emptiness. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Let $K=L_0\cap L_1$, now nonempty and finite. Choose pairwise disjoint small metric neighborhoods of its finitely many points. By step 2.1 every sufficiently far tail image lies in their union. That tail source $[S,\infty)\times[0,1]$ is connected, its continuous image is connected, and therefore it lies wholly in one of those neighborhoods, say the one about $x_+$. Within that chosen neighborhood the only possible cluster point is $x_+$ by step 2.1 and separation from the other points of $K$. Compactness now implies uniform convergence of the tail image to $x_+$: a sequence failing it would have a different subsequential cluster point. This proves the asserted uniform endpoint convergence; the derivative convergence was established in step 1.1. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of a limit in a metric space. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 For the transverse assertion, choose smooth local parametrizations $f_0,f_1$ of $L_0,L_1$ about an intersection point. The derivative of $(a,b)\mapsto f_0(a)-f_1(b)$ in a target coordinate chart is invertible because the two tangent spaces are complementary. By [F2] the zero of this difference is isolated. Thus the compact set $K$ is discrete. An infinite compact set has an accumulation point, which here would again lie in $K$ and contradict isolatedness; equivalently its isolating neighborhoods have a finite subcover. Hence $K$ is finite. At a negative strip end apply the same argument to $v(s,t)=u(-s,t)$, whose equation has almost complex coefficient $-J(-s,t,x)$ and fixed totally real boundary structures $-J_{b,j}$; all norm and energy hypotheses persist. This proves the remaining assertions without presuming a diagonal linear normal form or an exponential rate. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice and the actual finite-energy half-strip hypotheses of [[lem-finite-energy-transverse-strip-end-convergence]]. Suppose additionally that at each point $x\in L_0\cap L_1$ there is a smooth target coordinate chart $q_x$ centered at $x$, taking the two boundary submanifolds locally to
$$\mathbb R^m,\qquad \prod_{j=1}^m e^{i\theta_j(x)}\mathbb R,\qquad 0<\theta_j(x)<\pi,$$
and taking $J(s,t,\cdot)$ to the constant structure $i$ throughout that neighborhood for all source $s,t$. These are concrete geometric choice hypotheses, not moduli-space axioms.

Let $x_+$ be the end limit. On a sufficiently far tail put $v=q_{x_+}\circ u$ and $\gamma_+=\min_j(\pi-\theta_j(x_+))>0$. For every integer $k\ge0$ there is $C_k<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le1}|D^k v(s,t)|\le C_k e^{-\gamma_+s}.$$
For every $0\le\delta<\gamma_+$ and every finite $k$, the map $e^{\delta s}v$ belongs to $H^k$ on a far tail. Thus all derivatives converge exponentially to the constant generator. Constructing the prescribed coordinate charts and an admissible global $J$ with these values is a separate prerequisite.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The finite-energy actual strip, its compact geometric bounds, and the stated exact product-integrable neighborhoods.

[F1] [[lem-finite-energy-transverse-strip-end-convergence]] proves actual uniform convergence to a unique intersection point and uniform first-derivative convergence to zero.

[F2] The full twisted real Fourier construction in [[lem-transverse-linear-strip-cauchy-riemann-isomorphism]] proves that on one complex coordinate with real lower boundary and $e^{i\theta}\mathbb R$ upper boundary, $\phi_n(t)=e^{-i\lambda_nt}$, $\lambda_n=\pi n-\theta$, is an orthonormal basis of $L^2([0,1];\mathbb C)$ viewed as a real Hilbert space. Integration by parts with those boundary values makes $i\partial_t$ symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_n$. Parseval also gives $\|f\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|f_t\|_2$ for smooth boundary-compatible $f$, where $\gamma=\min\{\theta,\pi-\theta\}$.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 By [F1], after some $S$ the entire tail image is in the chart about $x_+$. Its coordinate map $v$ has exact boundary values in the two given product planes and satisfies $v_s+iv_t=0$. Coordinate and Riemannian derivative norms are uniformly comparable there after shrinking the neighborhood around the limit. Thus $\int_S^\infty\int_0^1(|v_s|^2+|v_t|^2)<\infty$. Apply the slice Poincare estimate in [F2] coordinatewise and integrate in $s$; it follows that $v\in L^2([S,\infty)\times[0,1])$. This use of finite energy excludes nondecaying modes without assuming a weighted space in advance. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Expand each coordinate in the real orthonormal basis of [F2]: $$v_j(s,t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{jn}(s)e^{-i\lambda_{jn}t},\qquad\lambda_{jn}=\pi n-\theta_j.$$ Its real coefficients are smooth in $s$ by differentiating their integral formula. Integration by parts in $t$ has zero real boundary form: at each edge both $v_j$ and the eigenfunction lie in its same real line. Projecting $v_s+iv_t=0$ consequently gives $$a_{jn}'+\lambda_{jn}a_{jn}=0,\qquad a_{jn}(s)=c_{jn}e^{-\lambda_{jn}(s-S)}.$$ Every mode coefficient is square-integrable in $s$ by step 1.1 and the norm-one coefficient functional. Since no $\lambda_{jn}$ is zero, this forces $c_{jn}=0$ whenever $\lambda_{jn}<0$. Parseval at $S$ gives $\sum_{j,n}|c_{jn}|^2=\|v(S,\cdot)\|_2^2<\infty$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 All surviving eigenvalues are positive and at least $\gamma_+$. For any integer $k\ge0$ and $h=s-S\ge1$, $$\sum_{j,n:\lambda_{jn}>0}\lambda_{jn}^{2k}e^{-2\lambda_{jn}h}\le e^{-2\gamma_+h}\sum_{j,n:\lambda_{jn}>0}\lambda_{jn}^{2k}e^{-2(\lambda_{jn}-\gamma_+)}<\infty.$$ The last constant is finite because these eigenvalues are a finite union of arithmetic progressions with spacing $\pi$. Each mixed derivative of order $k$ of a Fourier term has modulus at most $|c_{jn}|\lambda_{jn}^ke^{-\lambda_{jn}h}$. Cauchy-Schwarz and step 2.1 therefore show that the differentiated series converges absolutely and uniformly for $h\ge1$, with supremum at most $C_k e^{-\gamma_+h}\|v(S,\cdot)\|_2$. The same argument at every derivative order permits termwise differentiation on smaller open tails. The undifferentiated series already equals $v$ in $L^2$ on each slice by completeness; continuity identifies it everywhere, including boundary values, and its uniformly convergent derivatives equal the actual derivatives of $v$. Absorbing the fixed factor $e^{\gamma_+S}$ gives the asserted estimates. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Finally every derivative of $e^{\delta s}v$ up to a fixed order is a finite linear combination of $e^{\delta s}$ times derivatives from step 3.1. Its square is bounded by $C e^{-2(\gamma_+-\delta)s}$ on the tail, integrable because $\delta<\gamma_+$. This proves membership in every claimed weighted $H^k$ space. The argument proves exponential asymptotics of actual strips for the stated exact local geometric choice and supplies no global extension of that choice, index formula, or universal regularity assertion. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented smooth surface with positive area form $\eta$ and an orientation-compatible complex structure $j$. Use its smooth complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$, $m\ge1$, and the descended product symplectic form $\omega$ off the diagonal. Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m$ be disjoint embedded circles, and likewise $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$, with every alpha-beta intersection transverse. Let $T_\alpha,T_\beta\subset X$ be their product tori. Fix finitely many points $p$ of $\Sigma$ away from all these circles and the associated divisors $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$.

The intersection $K=T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$ is finite and disjoint from the diagonal and all $E_p$. There exist pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $U_x$ of its points, with closures disjoint from those protected sets, and smooth coordinate charts $q_x$ centered at $x$ taking $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ to $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$. There is a smooth almost complex structure $J_*$ on $X$ equal to $\operatorname{Sym}^m(j)$ near the diagonal and all $E_p$, taming $\omega$ elsewhere, and exactly $i$ in each $q_x$ chart near $x$.

More generally any smooth family $J_t$ with the first two properties can be modified inside the $U_x$, retaining its values outside them and near all protected sets, to have those exact product-integrable values on smaller neighborhoods for every $t$. The constant path $J_*$ therefore provides a genuine admissible geometric choice with the local hypotheses needed for product-integrable end asymptotics. No regularity or moduli count is asserted for that path.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The surface, symmetric product, product form, two curve systems, and finite protected points of the statement. The complex symmetric product and its ordinary off-diagonal unordered-product charts are part of this setup.

[F1] The actual finite-dimensional proofs in [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] and [[thm-higher-regularity-of-local-inverses]] supply the smooth local coordinate inverses used below.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 Two transverse embedded curves on a compact surface have finitely many intersections. Each crossing is isolated by [F1] applied to the difference of their local parametrizations in a surface chart, whose derivative is invertible by transversality. Their intersection is closed and compact, so the isolating neighborhoods have a finite subcover and the intersection is finite. There are only finitely many pairs of curves. A generator in $T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$ consists of one point on each alpha circle and one on each beta circle, so it is selected from that finite union of crossings; hence $K$ is finite. Its coordinates are distinct because the alpha circles are disjoint. None is a protected point $p$ because those lie off all circles. Thus $K$ avoids the diagonal and the divisors $E_p$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 We prove a pointwise interpolation formula. In a real symplectic vector space let $J_0$ be compatible, write $g_0(v,w)=\omega(v,J_0w)$, and let $J$ be any $\omega$-tame complex structure. Set $A=-J_0J$. The operator $A+I$ is invertible: a vector in its kernel would satisfy $Jv=-J_0v$, contrary to positive $\omega(v,Jv)$ for nonzero $v$. Define $B=(A-I)(A+I)^{-1}$. The relation $AJ_0A=J_0$, obtained directly from $J^2=J_0^2=-I$, gives $J_0^{-1}AJ_0=A^{-1}$ and hence $J_0^{-1}BJ_0=-B$. Thus $B$ anticommutes with $J_0$. Also $I-B=2(A+I)^{-1}$ is invertible and $A=(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}$. For $v=(I-B)w$ we have $$\omega(v,Jv)=g_0(v,Av)=g_0((I-B)w,(I+B)w)=|w|_{g_0}^2-|Bw|_{g_0}^2.$$ Tameness therefore gives $|Bw|_{g_0}<|w|_{g_0}$ for every nonzero $w$. The unit sphere is compact, so $\|B\|_{g_0}<1$. No symmetry of $B$ is assumed or needed. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 At a surface crossing $r$, choose parametrizations $a(x),b(y)$ of the two unique local curves with $a(0)=b(0)=r$, in any smooth surface coordinate chart.
