Choose a compact exhaustion $K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\cdots$ of $\Omega'$ with $K_j\subseteq\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}$ and cutoffs $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\Omega';[0,1])$ equal to $1$ on $K_j$; then $\chi_jv\to v$ pointwise everywhere and $|\chi_jv-v|^{p'}\le2^{p'}|v|^{p'}\in L^1(\Omega')$, so [F5] gives $\|\chi_jv-v\|_{L^{p'}}\to0$, and for $j$ large $\chi_jv\in C_c^\infty(\Omega')$ lies within $\eta$ of $f$. [F5, F6]

2.1 By [F3] the classes $\delta_{-h}^i\varphi$ converge pointwise as $h\to0$ to $\partial_i\varphi$ and are bounded in absolute value by $\|D\varphi\|_\infty$; choose a fixed compact neighbourhood $K\Subset\Omega$ containing $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ and all its translates by $te_i$ for sufficiently small $|t|$. The support of every such $\delta_{-h}^i\varphi$ lies in $K$, and $u\in L^1(K)$ by Hölder, so $\mathbf1_K|u|\,\|D\varphi\|_\infty$ is an integrable majorant on $\Omega$, and [F5] gives $$-\int_\Omega u\,\delta_{-h}^i\varphi\,dx\longrightarrow-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx=:\ell(\varphi).$$ Thus the limit exists for every test function, and step 1.1 identifies it with $\lim_{h\to0}\int_{\Omega'}\delta_h^iu\,\varphi\,dx$. [F3, F5, F9, step 1.1]

3.1 For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega')$ the hypothesis and Hölder give, for all $0<|h|<\min(h_0,h_1)$, $$\Big|\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,\varphi\,dx\Big|=\Big|\int_{\Omega'}\delta_h^iu\,\varphi\,dx\Big|\le\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\,\|\varphi\|_{L^{p'}(\Omega')}\le C\,\|\varphi\|_{L^{p'}(\Omega')};$$ passing to the limit along $h\to0$ in step 2.1 yields $|\ell(\varphi)|\le C\|\varphi\|_{L^{p'}(\Omega')}$. Hence $\ell$ is a $\mathbb K$-linear functional on the subspace $C_c^\infty(\Omega')$ of $L^{p'}(\Omega')$, bounded there with constant $C$. [F4, step 2.1, given]

4.1 By step 1.2 and the boundedness of step 3.1, $\ell$ has a unique extension to a bounded linear functional $\Lambda$ on $L^{p'}(\Omega')$ with $\|\Lambda\|\le C$: for $f\in L^{p'}(\Omega')$ choose test functions $\varphi_j\to f$; the values $\ell(\varphi_j)$ form a Cauchy sequence because $|\ell(\varphi_j)-\ell(\varphi_k)|\le C\|\varphi_j-\varphi_k\|$, and $\Lambda(f):=\lim_j\ell(\varphi_j)$ is independent of the approximating sequence. [step 3.1, step 1.2]

5.1 Apply [F7] with $q=p'$ (so that $q'=p$) to the functional $\Lambda$ on $L^{p'}(\Omega')$: for $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ the real duality theorem, and for $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$ the complex-linear duality lemma, provide a class $w\in L^p(\Omega';\mathbb K)$ with $$\Lambda(g)=\int_{\Omega'}w\,g\,dx\qquad(g\in L^{p'}(\Omega')),\qquad \|w\|_{L^p(\Omega')}=\|\Lambda\|\le C .$$ [F7, step 4.1]

6.1 For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega')$ (so that $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\Subset\Omega$ and $\partial_i\varphi$ has the same support) steps 2.1 and 5.1 give $$\int_{\Omega'}u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx=-\ell(\varphi)=-\Lambda(\varphi)=-\int_{\Omega'}w\,\varphi\,dx .$$ By [F8] this is exactly the weak-derivative identity, so $w$ is the weak derivative $D_iu$ of $u$ on $\Omega'$ and $\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$. [F8, step 2.1, step 5.1]

7.1 It remains to remove the test-function restriction in the convergence. Let $\varphi\in L^{p'}(\Omega')$ and $\eta>0$; by step 1.2 choose $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega')$ with $\|\varphi-\psi\|_{L^{p'}}<\eta/(2C+2\|w\|_{L^p}+1)$, and then $0<|h|$ small enough that $\big|\int_{\Omega'}\delta_h^iu\,\psi\,dx-\int_{\Omega'}w\,\psi\,dx\big|<\eta/2$, which is possible by steps 2.1 and 5.1. For such $h$, $$\Big|\int_{\Omega'}\delta_h^iu\,\varphi-\int_{\Omega'}w\,\varphi\Big|\le\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p}\|\varphi-\psi\|_{L^{p'}}+\Big|\int_{\Omega'}(\delta_h^iu-w)\psi\Big|+\|w\|_{L^p}\|\psi-\varphi\|_{L^{p'}}<\eta ,$$ using [F4] twice and the uniform bound of the hypothesis. Hence $\int_{\Omega'}\delta_h^iu\,\varphi\to\int_{\Omega'}w\,\varphi$ for every $\varphi\in L^{p'}(\Omega')$, which with step 6.1 proves the weak convergence $\delta_h^iu\rightharpoonup D_iu$ in $L^p(\Omega')$. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

Source notes.exact_text: Hunter's Theorem 4.53(2) (printed pp. 125-126) and Laugesen's Proposition 5.7(ii) (printed pp. 110-111) prove the same criterion by extracting a weak limit through Banach-Alaoglu; the route above replaces that extraction by the bounded functional $\varphi\mapsto-\int u\,\partial_i\varphi$ and the duality representation of [F7], so no weak compactness is used and the only choice principle consumed is Countable Choice, as the duality suppliers themselves record. Simon's Lecture 5, Lemma 7 states the convergence of difference quotients to weak derivatives in the form used in [F3].

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a smooth real rank-$2m$ vector bundle on $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, with a smooth endomorphism $J$ satisfying $J^2=-I$. On the two boundary edges let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth real rank-$m$ subbundles with $F_j\cap JF_j=0$. Suppose that outside a compact strip there are specified smooth complex frames $\tau_\pm:\mathbb C^m\to E$, intertwining $i$ and $J$, in which $F_0=\mathbb R^m$ and $F_1=i\mathbb R^m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real linear first-order operator on sections of $E$ with symbol
$$P(f\xi)=fP\xi+f_s\xi+f_tJ\xi$$
for every smooth real function $f$, and suppose its expression in each end frame is exactly $\partial_s+i\partial_t$ outside a compact strip.

There exist a global smooth complex frame $\Phi$, a sign matrix $S_+=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,1,\ldots,1)$ with $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$, an integer $\ell$, and a smooth real function $\vartheta(s)$, constant at $\pi/2$ on the negative end and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$ on the positive end, such that $\Phi=\tau_-$ on the negative end, $\Phi=\tau_+S_+$ on the positive end, and
$$F_0=\Phi\mathbb R^m,\qquad F_1=\Phi\left(e^{i\vartheta(s)}\mathbb R\times i\mathbb R^{m-1}\right).$$
In this frame $P$ is $\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t)$ with smooth compactly supported real linear $B$. On the $H^1$ completion of compactly supported smooth sections satisfying those actual boundary subbundles, with the norm defined by finite bundle charts on a compact core and the prescribed frames on the ends, $P$ maps to the corresponding $L^2(E)$ space and is real Fredholm, with
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P=-\ell.$$
The same index holds with the weight $e^{\delta|s|}$ for $0\le\delta<\pi/2$. These are indices before any translation quotient. The integer $\ell$ is independent of the choices in the construction, since it is minus the index of this fixed operator.

In particular the conclusion applies to the actual linearization at a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip of finite Dirichlet energy, measured in a smooth target metric, in a compact target, with compact totally real boundary submanifolds of transverse finite intersection, whenever the chosen target charts at their intersections identify those submanifolds with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t$ with the constant structure $i$ for every $t$. For product Heegaard tori such a geometric choice is available by the product-integrable generator-neighborhood construction. No domain Euler-measure formula, corner/excision theorem, generic regularity, or moduli count is part of this conclusion.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The smooth complex bundle, its totally real edge subbundles, two specified product end frames, and the actual first-order operator with the stated symbol and exact end expressions; Countable Choice.

[F1] A smooth invertible complex matrix loop bounds a smooth invertible disk map exactly when its determinant winding vanishes, including extension relative to prescribed smooth collar data ([[lem-complex-frame-loop-extension-determinant-winding]]).

[F2] A constant-principal strip operator on a given rotating scalar/product real-line boundary, with zeroth-order term tending to zero, is Fredholm with real index equal to the sum of the two endpoint angle floor differences. The same index holds for two-sided weights below the limiting spectral gap ([[lem-scalar-totally-real-strip-boundary-winding-index]]).

[F3] Actual finite-energy strips under the compact uniform smooth and totally real boundary hypotheses converge uniformly at each end to one of the transverse intersection points ([[lem-finite-energy-transverse-strip-end-convergence]]).

[F4] For the specified product Heegaard tori there are disjoint generator charts with the tori exactly $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and a global allowed $J_t$ equal to $i$ there for every $t$, preserving the diagonal/divisor neighborhoods and tameness elsewhere ([[lem-product-integrable-generator-neighborhoods-and-relative-tame-extension]]).

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 **A complex frame on a compact core, constructed rather than assumed.** Choose $R$ large enough that the stated end frames and exact operator expressions hold on neighborhoods of the vertical edges of the rectangle $Q=[-R,R]\times[0,1]$. The complex bundle on this rectangle has a finite complex-chart cover: locally choose $m$ real vectors whose images with their $J$ multiples form a basis at a point; their linear independence persists nearby, giving a complex chart. Compactness gives finitely many such charts $g_a:E\to\mathbb C^m$ and smooth nonnegative bumps $\beta_a$ supported in them with $\sum_a\beta_a^2>0$. These bumps can be made from finitely many smaller coordinate rectangles using the ordinary explicit smooth bump on a Euclidean ball. The map $I_x(v)=(\beta_a(x)g_a(v))_a$ embeds each fiber complex linearly in one fixed $\mathbb C^N$; zero extension is smooth because each bump has support inside its chart. Orthogonal projection $Q_x$ onto its image is smooth: in a local complex frame with image-column matrix $V_x$, it is $V_x(V_x^*V_x)^{-1}V_x^*$. Fix a basis in the image at one point $x_0$ of the rectangle and transport it to $x$ along $x_r=x_0+r(x-x_0)$ by the matrix equation $Z_r=[(Q_{x_r})_r,Q_{x_r}]Z$. The coefficient is skew-Hermitian. The identity $Q Q_r Q=0$, obtained by differentiating $Q^2=Q$, shows that a transported vector initially in the image stays in the image. Its norm and all inner products are preserved. The iterated-integral series has term bounds $M^n/n!$ on the compact parameter set; differentiating in $x$ adds only polynomial factors in $n$ and finite derivative bounds, so it gives a smooth family and a unique solution. Pulling the transported basis back by $I_x$ yields a smooth complex frame $\Psi$ on the whole rectangle. Thus contractibility of the base has not been substituted for a relative boundary framing argument. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Real frames and their endpoint orientation signs.** In $\Psi$ coordinates each $F_j$ is a smooth real rank-$m$ subbundle of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ along an interval. Its real orthogonal projection $Q_j(s)$ is smooth by the same finite matrix formula. The real equation $h'_j=[Q'_j,Q_j]h_j$, starting with any ordered basis in its initial fiber, transports a smooth real basis along the whole edge, by the same series and projection identities as in step 1.1. Start the lower basis at $\tau_-\mathbb R^m$ and the upper basis at $\tau_- i\mathbb R^m$. On the positive end compare the transported lower basis with $\tau_+$ and the transported upper basis with $\tau_+ i$. Let their real determinant signs be $\sigma_0,\sigma_1\in\{1,-1\}$. Set $S_+=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_0,1,\ldots,1)$ and choose the unique $p\in\{0,1\}$ with $\sigma_0(-1)^p=\sigma_1$. The desired lower terminal basis $\tau_+S_+$ and upper terminal basis $\tau_+S_+\operatorname{diag}(i(-1)^p,i,\ldots,i)$ then have the same orientations as the respective transported bases. We may correct the transported bases by smooth real matrices to obtain frames $f_0(s),f_1(s)$ equal to those specified bases on entire end collars, and to the initial specified bases on the negative collar. Here is the needed path construction: real matrices of positive determinant can be joined to the identity using row-addition paths $I+t cE_{ab}$ to diagonalize, positive diagonal rescalings, and planar rotations removing pairs of negative diagonal entries. A zero pivot can first be made nonzero by adding a row with a nonzero entry, so no row permutation of negative determinant is required. There are finitely many steps. On each end collar the correction matrix has positive determinant; flatten its source coordinate on an inner collar, join its resulting constant value to the identity by this finite path, and retain its original values on a smaller outer collar. This matches all derivatives where pieces are pasted. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The boundary frame loop and its actual obstruction.** Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi(s)$ equal to zero on the negative collar and one on the positive collar. First put $\vartheta_0(s)=\pi/2+p\pi\chi(s)$. Prescribe a complex frame along the rectangle boundary as follows: on the bottom it is $f_0(s)$; on the top it is $f_1(s)\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\vartheta_0(s)},-i,\ldots,-i)$; on the left it is $\tau_-$; on the right it is $\tau_+S_+$. The columns of $f_j$ are complex linearly independent, since $F_j\cap JF_j=0$: a complex dependence has real and imaginary parts in $F_j$ whose $J$ images coincide, forcing both to vanish. Thus these are invertible complex frames. Their values agree on the corner collars by step 2.1. Express them in the global core frame $\Psi$ to obtain an invertible matrix loop $G$, oriented by $ds\wedge dt$ on the rectangle. Round the four corners inside their end-frame neighborhoods and use the already specified end frame along each rounded arc. This gives a smooth matrix loop on the rounded core; the old edge path and rounded arc are homotopic within that end neighborhood, so their determinant windings agree. Let $k=w(G)\in\mathbb Z$. The lower orientation correction alone has not forced this integer to vanish. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Absorb the winding and extend the frame relative to the ends.** Replace the top angle by $\vartheta(s)=\vartheta_0(s)-2\pi k\chi(s)$. The new top frame differs from the old one by $\operatorname{diag}(e^{2\pi i k\chi(s)},1,\ldots,1)$. The oriented top edge is traversed from $s=R$ to $s=-R$, so this changes determinant winding by $-k$. The new boundary loop therefore has winding zero; its negative and positive angle limits are $\pi/2$ and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$, where $\ell=p-2k$. It retains exactly the prescribed vertical frames because the added end phases are integer multiples of $2\pi$. Extend the boundary matrix data to a thin collar in $Q$, keeping them equal to $\Psi^{-1}\tau_-$ and $\Psi^{-1}\tau_+S_+$ on smaller vertical collars. Such collar data can be built locally by extending each edge matrix in its normal direction; near a corner the vertical data are already smooth invertible matrices on a full corner neighborhood and agree with the horizontal edge data. Shrink the remaining collars so all overlapping values lie in a small convex matrix ball contained in $\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb C)$, and patch with finitely many scalar bumps, retaining the exact edge and vertical values. The relative-collar part of [F1] now fills this zero-winding matrix map on the rounded core disk. Multiplying the filling by $\Psi$ and retaining the given end frames on the removed corner neighborhoods gives $\Phi$ on the whole core rectangle. It equals the specified vertical frames on collars, so extends to all $S$ by $\tau_-$ and $\tau_+S_+$ on the ends. Its two horizontal boundary frames give exactly the two subbundle identities in the Statement. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 **Identify the actual operator and Sobolev domains.** A finite collection of smooth bundle charts on the compact core, with compactly supported scalar cutoffs and the two given end frames, defines an $H^1$ norm on compactly supported smooth sections. Any two such choices give equivalent norms: chart transition matrices and their first derivatives are bounded on the finitely many compact overlaps, and outside the core both use the given end frames. The same argument applies to the $L^2$ target norm. Multiplication by $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ is bounded for these norms, because their matrices and first derivatives are bounded on the compact core and they are the constant comparisons $I,S_+$ on the ends. They send the actual compactly supported smooth boundary sections bijectively to the scalar/product-line sections prescribed by $\vartheta$, hence identify their completions. The symbol identity and $\Phi i=J\Phi$ show that $\Phi^{-1}P\Phi$ has principal part $\partial_s+i\partial_t$. To see this directly, write a section as a sum of the $2m$ real coordinate functions times $\Phi e_a$ and $J\Phi e_a$ and apply the stated real Leibniz identity to each summand. The remaining terms define a smooth real linear multiplication matrix $B$. On the ends $\Phi$ is the given end frame times the constant $I$ or $S_+$, and the operator there is exactly $D$; thus $B=0$ there. It is therefore compactly supported and bounded. This establishes the normal form for the actual operator and its domain, rather than assuming them from its principal symbol alone. [step 4.1, given, construct, algebra]

6.1 **Fredholm index and weights.** Apply [F2] to the operator of step 5.1. The first upper angle has end values $\pi/2$ and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$; every other angle is constantly $\pi/2$. The floor differences are consequently $0-\ell=-\ell$ for the first component and zero for the rest. Thus $P$ is Fredholm with real index $-\ell$. All limiting product-angle spectra have gap $\pi/2$, so [F2] also applies with every $0\le\delta<\pi/2$. The frame comparison commutes with the scalar weight and remains bounded on weighted completions by the same compact-core estimates. Source and target isomorphisms preserve kernel, range and cokernel, proving the weighted claim for $P$. Different choices of frames, real basis signs or filling which meet the same hypotheses still compute this fixed Fredholm operator's index, so they give the same integer $\ell$. Nothing has been subtracted for source translation. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Apply this to the actual geometric linearization.** Let $u$ be the smooth finite-energy strip in the last clause. By [F3], its two far ends lie in the specified generator charts. There the nonlinear equation is exactly $v_s+i v_t=0$ in target coordinates, so its coordinate linearization is exactly $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t$, with boundary variations in $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$. On the whole strip put $E=u^*TX$, $J(s,t)=J_t(u(s,t))$ and $F_j=u(\cdot,j)^*TL_j$. These are smooth bundles with $F_j\cap JF_j=0$ by the given totally real hypothesis. The coordinate formula for the actual real linearization at a solution is $P\xi=\xi_s+J_t(u)\xi_t+(dJ_t)_u[\xi]u_t$. It has exactly the stated symbol. These local formulas transform as a bundle operator: differentiating a change of target coordinates introduces its derivative on the Cauchy–Riemann section, whose value at this solution is zero, so no extra principal or residual term occurs. Equivalently the covariant and coordinate formulas agree after the corresponding source and target bundle identification. Thus all hypotheses of the frame, normal-form and index arguments above hold, proving the claimed actual real $H^1$ Fredholm theorem. For product Heegaard tori their Lagrangian tangent spaces are totally real for a tame $J$: a nonzero $v$ with $v,Jv$ both tangent would give $\omega(v,Jv)=0$, contradicting tameness. The geometric product charts and the simultaneous all-$t$ exact values of $J_t$ are supplied by [F4]. This completes the asserted application, while the equality with domain Euler measure and corner multiplicities still requires separate corner, excision and domain-comparison proofs. [F3, F4, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, and $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Write $X_0=H^1_\theta$ for the real $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in $s$ satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $B:S\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb C^m)$ be smooth up to the boundary, with every derivative bounded, and suppose its uniform end limits are real diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,j})$ with $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. For an integer $q\ge0$ put
$$X_q=H^{q+1}(S;\mathbb C^m)\cap X_0,\qquad Y_q=H^q(S;\mathbb C^m),\qquad T_q=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B:X_q\longrightarrow Y_q,$$
using real Hilbert spaces and their indicated Sobolev norms. There are no higher boundary conditions: only the zeroth trace encoded by $X_0$ is required. In particular no normal derivative or forcing trace is prescribed.

Every $T_q$ is bounded Fredholm. Its kernel is the same set as the kernel of $T_0$, and its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}T_0$. The inclusion of $Y_q$ in $L^2$ induces an isomorphism of real cokernels. Thus
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T_q=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T_0=\sum_j\left(\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{-,j}}\pi\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{+,j}}\pi\right\rfloor\right).$$
More precisely, if $u\in X_0$ and $T_0u=f\in H^q$, then $u\in X_q$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q\bigl(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|u\|_{H^1}\bigr).$$

The same conclusions hold with smooth two-sided weights $w=e^{\delta\rho(s)}$, where $\rho$ is smooth, equals $|s|$ outside a compact interval, has all derivatives of positive order bounded, and $0\le\delta<\min_{\pm,j,n}|\pi n-\theta_j+b_{\pm,j}|$. Weighted spaces mean $wu\in X_q$ and $wf\in Y_q$. Their index is the same displayed index. The weight is smooth at zero even for $q\ge1$.

Finally, for an actual geometric strip operator with exact product-integrable ends and the smooth bundle frame supplied by the geometric strip normal-form theorem, the actual $H^{q+1}$ boundary-section domain and $H^q$ target have this same real index before translation quotient, also with these smooth weights. This asserts integer Hilbert Sobolev agreement; no $W^{1,p}$ comparison or Heegaard-domain Euler formula is asserted.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** Countable Choice and the spaces, smooth coefficient bounds, limiting nondegenerate diagonal matrices and weights in the Statement.

[F1] The constant strip operator $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t:X_0\to L^2$ is an isomorphism with $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C\|Dv\|_2$; its modal proof also identifies $X_0$ as a closed subspace of the usual $H^1$ space ([[lem-transverse-linear-strip-cauchy-riemann-isomorphism]]).

[F2] The operator $T_0$ is Fredholm; the proof constructs orthogonal projections onto closed subspaces of real Hilbert spaces using Countable Choice and a minimizing sequence ([[lem-variable-zero-order-strip-cauchy-riemann-fredholm]]).

[F3] The real $H^1$ index is the displayed sum of endpoint floor differences, with unchanged index for two-sided weights below the limiting spectral gap ([[lem-diagonal-strip-cauchy-riemann-fredholm-index]]).

[F4] For the actual geometric operator there is a smooth complex frame with prescribed product-integrable ends which identifies its $H^1$ boundary domain with a rotating product-line domain and its operator with $D$ plus a smooth compactly supported zeroth-order term. The rotation becomes fixed product lines by multiplication by $U(s,t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{ia(s)t},1,\ldots,1)$ with $a$ smooth and constant on the ends ([[lem-geometric-strip-linearization-frame-and-fredholm-index]], with its explicit scalar gauge).

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 **Weak derivatives from bounded tests.** We first record the precise Hilbert argument used below. If a distribution $v$ is in $L^2$ and $|\int v\,\partial_j\phi|\le M\|\phi\|_2$ for all smooth compact interior tests, this functional extends uniquely to the closure of that test space in $L^2$, which is all of $L^2$. The density assertion follows by cutting off in $s$, removing boundary strips of width tending to zero, and convolving on the resulting interior rectangles; convergence is first checked for step functions and then in $L^2$. By the orthogonal projection construction in [F2], every bounded real functional $L$ on a Hilbert space has a representing vector: if $L\ne0$, take $z$ with $L(z)\ne0$, put $z_\perp=z-\operatorname{proj}_{\ker L}z$, and write $x-(L(x)/L(z_\perp))z_\perp\in\ker L$. This gives $L(x)=L(z_\perp)\langle x,z_\perp\rangle/\|z_\perp\|^2$; the zero functional is represented by zero. Hence $v$ has weak derivative in $L^2$ of norm at most $M$. In particular, if $v_h\to v$ in $L^2$ and $\|v_h\|_{H^1}\le M$, then $v\in H^1$ with the corresponding bounds. Integration against interior tests proves each derivative assertion; approximating any $L^2$ test by smooth ones proves weak convergence of the derivatives, and therefore weak $H^1$ convergence. A closed Hilbert subspace is weakly closed, since pairing with its orthogonal complement vanishes and the orthogonal projection decomposition is exhaustive. These arguments use only the Countable-Choice projections of [F2]. [F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 **A tangential difference quotient keeps exactly the permitted boundary condition.** For $u\in X_0$ and $h\ne0$ set $\delta_hu(s,t)=(u(s+h,t)-u(s,t))/h$. Translation and subtraction preserve $X_0$, first on its defining smooth maps and then by completion. The fundamental theorem of calculus in $s$, followed by Cauchy–Schwarz and integration, gives $\|\delta_hu\|_2\le\|u_s\|_2$. It also proves $\delta_hu\to u_s$ strongly in $L^2$ by approximation in $H^1$ by the defining smooth maps. The same argument gives $\|\delta_hf\|_2\le\|f_s\|_2$ for $f\in H^1$, by interior approximation and the usual one-dimensional slicing identity, which itself follows by integrating the weak derivative against product tests. If $T_0u=f\in H^1$, put $B_h(s,t)=B(s+h,t)$. The weak product rule, obtained by testing and smooth approximation, gives $D\delta_hu=\delta_hf-B_h\delta_hu-(\delta_h B)u$. Since $\|\delta_hB\|_\infty\le\|B_s\|_\infty$, [F1] yields $\|\delta_hu\|_{H^1}\le C(\|f_s\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u_s\|_2+\|B_s\|_\infty\|u\|_2)$ uniformly for $h\ne0$. By step 1.1, $u_s\in H^1$ with this bound. It belongs to $X_0$ by weak closedness, because every difference quotient does. This is why no differentiated normal boundary condition has been imposed. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Recover the normal derivatives and iterate.** The equation gives $u_t=-i(f-Bu-u_s)$. For $f\in H^1$ the right side is in $H^1$ by step 2.1 and the bounded first derivatives of $B$. Thus both $u_s,u_t\in H^1$, giving $u\in H^2$ and the claimed estimate for $q=1$. For the induction suppose the conclusion is known for order $q-1\ge1$ and $f\in H^q$. The already proved lower orders give $u\in H^q$ and $u_s\in X_0$. Differentiating distributionally gives $T_0u_s=f_s-B_su\in H^{q-1}$. Apply the order-$q-1$ result to this equation, to get $u_s\in H^q$ with its bound. The formula for $u_t$ then gives $u_t\in H^q$. All weak derivatives of order at most $q+1$ are therefore in $L^2$. The Leibniz rule and the finitely many bounded derivatives of $B$ give $\|u\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|u\|_{H^1})$ by the induction bounds. The case $q=0$ is immediate. The argument has differentiated only in the tangential direction before using the equation to recover normal derivatives. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Identify range and cokernel, not just nullspaces.** The space $X_q$ is a closed real subspace of $H^{q+1}$: convergence there implies convergence in $H^1$, where $X_0$ is closed by [F1]. It is Hilbert, and the bounded derivatives of $B$ make $T_q$ bounded. Step 3.1 with $f=0$ proves $\ker T_q=\ker T_0$. The same step for arbitrary $f\in Y_q$ proves $\operatorname{Ran}T_q=Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}T_0$. This range is closed in $Y_q$ because $\operatorname{Ran}T_0$ is closed in $L^2$ by [F2]. The quotient map $Y_q\to L^2/\operatorname{Ran}T_0$ is surjective: smooth compactly supported interior functions are dense in $L^2$ by the explicit approximation in step 1.1 and belong to $Y_q$, so its image is dense; the image is a linear subspace of a finite-dimensional space and hence closed, as follows by choosing a basis and the finite-dimensional Euclidean lower norm bound. Its kernel is precisely $\operatorname{Ran}T_q$. This proves the asserted cokernel isomorphism and Fredholmness. Both kernel and cokernel dimensions agree with $q=0$, and [F3] gives the displayed index. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Smooth weights.** Put $v=wu$. Direct differentiation gives $wT_0w^{-1}v=Dv+(B-\delta\rho')v$. This new coefficient has all derivatives bounded and real diagonal limits $b_{-,j}+\delta$ and $b_{+,j}-\delta$. The spectral-gap bound ensures that no limiting eigenvalue crosses zero when $\delta$ is increased from zero to its stated value; hence the endpoint floors in [F3] stay constant. Apply steps 2.1–4.1 to this conjugated operator. Multiplication by $w$ is an isometric identification by the definitions of the weighted spaces and preserves their real-line boundary conditions. Thus it transfers all kernel, range, cokernel and regularity assertions, as well as the index. Smoothness of $\rho$ at zero is essential for this high-order argument. At order one these spaces agree with those defined using $e^{\delta|s|}$ up to equivalent norms, since the ratio and its reciprocal are bounded Lipschitz functions constant outside a compact interval. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 **Transfer to the actual geometric operator.** In [F4] the frame matrices on a finite compact core are smooth, and their comparisons on the two ends are constant; every derivative is bounded. The extra scalar/product gauge $U$ has all derivatives bounded because its angle is smooth and constant outside a compact interval, while $0\le t\le1$. Its inverse has the same property. The repeated Leibniz rule therefore makes frame and gauge multiplication bounded isomorphisms on each of the finitely charted geometric $H^r$ spaces for every integer $r\ge0$. They identify precisely the zeroth boundary trace, without restricting any higher derivative. After these transformations the actual operator has fixed product-line domain and a smooth zeroth-order coefficient with all derivatives bounded and real diagonal end limits; the scalar gauge contributes $-a+i a't$, whose limits are real. Thus steps 3.1–5.1 apply to the actual $H^{q+1}\to H^q$ operator, including the smooth weighted realizations. The transformations commute with scalar weights. The resulting common real index is the actual $H^1$ index supplied by [F4], and nothing has been subtracted for translations. [F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

Statement.exact_text:
Assume countable choice. Let $E,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $f$ a $C^1$ map on an open neighborhood of the closed ball $\overline B_E(0,r)$, and $D=df(0)$. Suppose a specified bounded linear map $Q:Y\to E$ satisfies $DQ=I_Y$. Fix $M>0$, $L\ge0$ with $\|Q\|\le M$ and
$$\|df(x)-df(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\quad(x,y\in\overline B_E(0,r)).$$
Put $\varepsilon=\|f(0)\|$. If
$$2M\varepsilon<r,\qquad MLr\le\tfrac12,$$
then there is a unique $x\in\operatorname{im}Q\cap\overline B_E(0,r)$ with $f(x)=0$. It satisfies
$$\|x\|\le2M\varepsilon,\qquad \|x+Qf(0)\|\le2M^3L\varepsilon^2.$$
The sequence $x_0=0$,
$$x_{n+1}=-Qf(0)-Q\bigl(f(x_n)-f(0)-Dx_n\bigr)$$
converges to this correction, with contraction ratio at most $1/2$. At the corrected zero $df(x)$ is still surjective, with specified right inverse
$$Q_x=Q\bigl[I_Y+(df(x)-D)Q\bigr]^{-1},\qquad \|Q_x\|\le2M.$$

The following local smooth conclusions also hold. If $f(0)=0$, $f$ is $C^q$, $1\le q\le\infty$, and $D$ has the specified bounded right inverse $Q$, continuity of $df$ alone suffices for a local $C^q$ zero-set chart. With $K=\ker D$ and $V=\operatorname{im}Q$, there is a $C^q$ map $v$ from a neighborhood of $0$ in $K$ to $V$, with $v(0)=dv(0)=0$, such that, in a product neighborhood for $E=K\oplus V$,
$$f(k+w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=v(k).$$
For a $C^q$ family $f(p,z)$, $p$ in any Banach parameter space, the same assertion holds locally with $v=v(p,k)$ whenever $f(p_0,0)=0$ and $d_zf(p_0,0)Q=I_Y$. In particular, if $Q(p)$ is a specified $C^q$ family of right inverses to $d_zf(p,0)$ and the quantitative hypotheses hold strictly with locally uniform constants, the unique corrections in $\operatorname{im}Q(p)$ depend $C^q$ on $p$.

This is an abstract correction and chart theorem. It assumes the right inverse and all displayed estimates; it supplies no geometric pregluing, uniform right-inverse construction, Fredholm index, or gluing exhaustion theorem.

Facts & Assumptions.exact_text:
**Given:** The complete real normed spaces, specified right inverse and quantitative or local smooth hypotheses in the Statement. Differentiability is in the norm-remainder sense and higher derivatives in operator norm.

[F1] [[def-banach-space]] supplies completeness. [[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]] and [[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]] fix the norm-remainder derivative and recursive continuous higher derivatives.

Proof.exact_text:
1.1 We first establish the needed mean-value estimate without selecting a dual functional. If a differentiable Banach-valued path $g$ on $[a,b]$ has $\|g'(t)\|\le C$, then $\phi(t)=\|g(t)-g(a)\|$ has upper right Dini derivative at most $C$, by the derivative remainder and the triangle inequality. For $\eta>0$, put $h(t)=\phi(t)-(C+\eta)(t-a)$. If $h(b)>h(a)$, its minimum on the compact interval is attained at some $t_0<b$; all sufficiently small right differences there are nonnegative, contradicting the strictly negative upper right Dini derivative. Thus $\phi(b)\le(C+\eta)(b-a)$; let $\eta\downarrow0$. Applying this argument to each subinterval proves the segment estimate $\|g(b)-g(a)\|\le C(b-a)$. For a continuous Banach-valued function, its dyadic Riemann sums are Cauchy by uniform continuity, hence converge by completeness; comparison with arbitrary fine partitions identifies the same integral. The difference-quotient estimate for this integral gives its derivative equal to the integrand. The segment estimate just proved makes a differentiable path with zero derivative constant. Consequently the Banach-valued fundamental theorem holds for $C^1$ paths. Applied to $N(z)=f(z)-f(0)-Dz$, it gives $$\|N(z)\|\le\tfrac{L}{2}\|z\|^2,\qquad \|N(z)-N(w)\|\le Lr\|z-w\|$$ on the closed radius-$r$ ball. The first bound integrates $\|(df(tz)-D)z\|\le Lt\|z\|^2$; the second uses the segment estimate and $\|dN\|\le Lr$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The operators $QD$ and $P=I_E-QD$ are bounded complementary projections: $(QD)^2=QD$, $DP=0$, $P|_{\ker D}=I$, and $QD$ is the identity on $V=\operatorname{im}Q$. Their ranges are closed, since a bounded projection's range is the kernel of its complementary projection. Thus $E=K\oplus V$, and the closed ball in $V$ is complete. On the radius-$\rho$ ball in $V$, $\rho=2M\varepsilon<r$, define $T(z)=-Qf(0)-QN(z)$. Step 1.1 and $MLr\le1/2$ give $$\|T(z)\|\le M\varepsilon+MLr\|z\|\le\rho,\qquad \|T(z)-T(w)\|\le\tfrac12\|z-w\|.$$ Starting with $x_0=0$, iterate this one prescribed map. Its increments are at most $2^{-n}\|x_1-x_0\|$, so the geometric tail bound makes the sequence Cauchy and complete convergence gives a fixed point $x$. If $\varepsilon=0$ the ball is the singleton zero and the same conclusion holds directly. On $V$, applying $D$ to $z=T(z)$ gives $Dz=-f(0)-N(z)$, hence $f(z)=0$; conversely every zero in $V$ satisfies this fixed-point identity because $QDz=z$. The Lipschitz estimate holds on the entire radius-$r$ ball, so any two zeros in that larger ball coincide as well. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The norm bound is $\|x\|\le\rho$. The equation $x+Qf(0)=-QN(x)$ and the quadratic bound of step 1.1 give $$\|x+Qf(0)\|\le\tfrac{ML}{2}\rho^2=2M^3L\varepsilon^2.$$ Write $A=(df(x)-D)Q$. Then $\|A\|\le LM\|x\|\le MLr\le1/2$. The explicit series $\sum_{n\ge0}(-A)^n$ converges in bounded-operator norm, since its tails have geometric norm bounds and the operator space is complete pointwise with the uniform limit bound. Multiplication of finite partial sums and passage to the limit show that it is a two-sided inverse of $I_Y+A$, of norm at most two. Therefore $df(x)Q_x=(I_Y+A)(I_Y+A)^{-1}=I_Y$, and $\|Q_x\|\le2M$. No choice of a new complement or inverse has been made. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 We prove the local chart, including its parameter version, directly. Replace $D$ by $d_zf(p_0,0)$, use the fixed splitting of step 2.1, and set $$T(p,k,w)=w-Qf(p,k+w),\qquad w\in V.$$ Its derivative in $w$ is $I_V-Qd_zf(p,k+w)|_V$, which vanishes at $(p_0,0,0)$. Choose product neighborhoods with $\|d_wT\|\le1/2$ there, by continuity. Choose a closed $V$-ball of radius $b>0$ inside this product, then shrink the open parameter and $K$ neighborhoods so $\|T(p,k,0)\|<b/2$. The segment estimate in step 1.1 makes $T(p,k,\cdot)$ a contraction of that closed ball into itself. Its explicit iteration from zero gives a unique fixed point $v(p,k)$. Since $Q$ is injective ($DQ=I$), the fixed-point equation is equivalent to $f(p,k+v)=0$. Any zero in the product neighborhood is that fixed point. The fixed point is interior because its norm is at most $2\|T(p,k,0)\|<b$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The fixed point depends continuously, and locally Lipschitz, on $(p,k)$. For two nearby parameters $a,a'$ denoting this combined variable, subtract the fixed-point equations to obtain $$\|v(a')-v(a)\|\le2\|T(a',v(a))-T(a,v(a))\|.$$ Continuity gives continuity; a bounded derivative in the parameter variable on a sufficiently small product ball gives local Lipschitz dependence by step 1.1. Put $H=I_V-d_wT(a,v(a))$. Its Neumann inverse has norm at most two. For a small parameter increment $h$, the $C^1$ remainder, and the Lipschitz bound on $v$, give $$H\bigl(v(a+h)-v(a)\bigr)=d_aT(a,v(a))h+o(\|h\|).$$ Thus $v$ is differentiable, with $$dv(a)=\bigl[I_V-d_wT(a,v(a))\bigr]^{-1}d_aT(a,v(a)).$$ All factors are continuous; hence $v$ is $C^1$. When there is no parameter $p$, at $k=0$ one has $v(0)=0$ and $d_kT=-QD|_K=0$, so $dv(0)=0$. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 For completeness, the derivative rules just used require no hidden selection principle. The chain rule follows by substituting the two norm-remainder expansions, with local boundedness of the first derivative controlling the inner remainder. The product rule follows by expanding a bounded bilinear product and bounding the product of the two increments. On the open set of invertible bounded operators, the identity $$ (A+H)^{-1}-A^{-1}=-(A+H)^{-1}HA^{-1}$$ and the Neumann norm bound show continuity; substituting it once more gives derivative $H\mapsto-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$ with quadratic remainder. Differentiating this finite product expression inductively proves smoothness of inversion. If $T$ is $C^q$, the derivative formula in step 4.1 is therefore $C^{j-1}$ whenever $v$ is $C^{j-1}$ and $j\le q$. Induction upgrades $v$ to $C^q$, including every finite order when $q=\infty$. These arguments also prove the smoothness of the explicit linear splitting coordinate maps and the resulting zero-set parametrization $k\mapsto k+v(k)$. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Finally suppose the right inverse varies smoothly with $p$. Work in the fixed space $Y$ and write the correction as $x=Q(p)y$. Put $D(p)=d_zf(p,0)$ and $N(p,z)=f(p,z)-f(p,0)-D(p)z$. The correction equation is exactly $$y=-f(p,0)-N(p,Q(p)y).$$ The right side also equals $y-f(p,Q(p)y)$, so it is $C^q$ without requiring an extra derivative of $D(p)$. At a fixed solution its derivative in $y$ has norm at most $LM\|x\|<1/2$. In a small product neighborhood of that fixed point and parameter, continuity gives a uniform contraction bound less than one. Shrink a closed ball about that fixed point and then the parameter neighborhood so the map preserves that ball, as in step 3.2. The local contraction and differentiability proof in the three preceding chart steps thus applies in $Y$ to give a $C^q$ family $y(p)$, hence $x(p)=Q(p)y(p)$. Uniqueness from step 2.1 identifies it with the quantitative correction. The zero target or zero kernel cases are included: the relevant ball is a singleton and the stated maps and formulas still apply. All infinite objects used were explicit convergent sequences or series, so no stronger choice axiom entered. This proves all assertions. [step 2.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, cases] ∎
